intervenor.

that he may be provided with legal aid counsel.

Supreme Court Legal Services Committee, through its Secretary, to
assign a legal aid counsel of reasonable standing at the Bar to the
applicant. The needful be done immediately.

been filed by the State of Uttarakhand.

appropriate Bench on 03.11.2026, after obtaining necessary orders
from Hon’ble the Chief Justice of India.

Interlocutory Applications filed by different applicants. Let those
applications also be listed in seriatim before the assigned Bench
on the date fixed.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
Delhi
I.A. No.296955/2026 in S.L.P . (C) No.16838 of 2025:
1. We see no reason to entertain this application, though the contention of
the applicants is that they have been in service for six and a half years. The
applicants were, if at all, selected pursuant to a notice issued in November,
2020 when the country was under the grip of COVID and that too on a daily
wage  basis.  Not  too  many  might  have  been  interested  in  offering  their
candidature. In our opinion, the applicants have no right to claim absorption;
hence, the interlocutory application stands dismissed.
2. As and when vacancies are advertised, the applicants shall be at liberty to
participate in the process.
I.A. No.299984/2026 in Writ Petition (Civil) No.132/2016:
3. Issue notice, returnable on 17th November, 2026.
4. Ms. Swati Ghildiyal, learned counsel accepts notice on behalf of the NCT of
Delhi. Service of formal notice, thus, stands dispensed with.
5. Counter affidavit may be filed within two weeks.
Madhya Pradesh

6. Apropos  our  order  dated  01st September,  2026,  the  State  of  Madhya
Pradesh  is  in  the  process  of  appointing  116  (one  hundred  and  sixteen)
(contractual) special teachers/guest teachers, who have been found to possess
both Rehabilitation Council of India1 and T eacher Eligibility T est2 qualifications. 
7. According to Mr. Sarthak Raizada, learned counsel for the State of Madhya
Pradesh, appointment letters have been issued to approximately 25 (twenty
five) (contractual) special teachers/guest teachers and the process in respect of
the  remaining  (contractual)  special  teachers/guest  teachers  would  be
completed roughly within six weeks. 
8. If  indeed,  these  116  (one  hundred  and  sixteen)  (contractual)  special
teachers/guest teachers have not been paid their salary since May, 2026, the
State shall look into their grievance and take such ameliorative steps as are
warranted on facts and in the circumstances. 
9. We need to hear the learned counsel for the Rehabilitation Council of India
as well as the National Council for T eacher Education 3 on the question as to
whether  TET  is  a  mandatory  qualification  for  appointment  as  teachers  in
primary  schools  even  for  children  with  special  needs.  Since  on  an  earlier
occasion,  learned  counsel  for  the  NCTE  had  expressed  her  difficulty  to  be
present today, we defer consideration of such question till 17th November, 2026.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
ORIGINAL CIVIL JURISDICTION
WRIT PETITION (C) NO. 369 OF 2022
YASH CHARITABLE TRUST & ORS.       …PETITIONER(S)
VERSUS
UNION OF INDIA & ORS.     …RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. In  our  Order  dated  01.09.2026,  we  had  posed  certain
questions to the respondents, to ascertain whether reasonable
and  genuine  steps  are  being  taken  by  the  regulatory
authorities,  the  treating  institutions  and  the  caregivers  to
move existing patients, wherever appropriate, towards a duly
regulated research / clinical trial framework.
2. We  heard  Ms.  Aishwarya  Bhati,  the  learned  Additional
Solicitor  General  appearing  for  the  Union  of  India.  She
highlighted the steps which have been and those which are
proposed to be taken, in compliance with the Judgment &
Order dated 30.01.2026. 
3. In today's hearing, we also heard Mr. Neeraj Kishan Kaul, the
learned Senior counsel appearing for the Respondent No.13

--- Page 119 ---
2
(Parents’ Forum for Stem Cells in Autism and Cerebral Palsy).
We also heard Mr. Prashant Bhushan, the learned counsel on
the subject.
4. We also heard certain individuals present in Court today, who
stated  that  they  are  appearing  in-person  to  voice  their
concerns  regarding  the  status  of  the  ongoing  stem  cell
therapies  for  Autism  Spectrum  Disorder  (ASD)  being
administered to their children or wards. 
5. At the outset, we consider it necessary to clarify the scope
and import of our Judgment & Order dated 30.01.2026. The
present proceedings are not concerned with determining the
efficacy of the so-called stem cell ‘therapies’ for ASD, nor is it
the endeavour of this Court to evaluate the scientific claims
advanced  by  various  individuals  in  support  of  such
intervention. The question before us is one of law, namely,
whether  the  administration  of  such  therapy  for  ASD  is
permissible  having  regard  to  the  applicable  regulatory
framework.
6. We would like to hereby reiterate that the therapeutic use of
stem cells for ASD is not recognised as ‘sound and relevant
medical practice’ by the concerned authorities in the light of
the scientific knowledge and regulatory standards prevailing
at  present.  Consequently,  medical  practitioners  who  offer
such intervention as a clinical service, outside an approved
and monitored research or clinical trial setting, fail to meet
the reasonable standard of care owed to their patients. It is on
this basis that we clarified the existing position of law. Under

--- Page 120 ---
3
the existing regulatory framework, stem cell ‘therapy’ for ASD
cannot be offered as a clinical service outside an approved
and  monitored  research/clinical  trial  setting.  In  such
circumstances, the individuals diagnosed with ASD, or their
parents/guardians/caregivers  cannot  demand  that  such  a
form  of  procedure  be  permitted  to  be  administered  as  a
clinical service. However, one would still have the liberty to
participate  in  an  approved  and  regulated  research/clinical
trial involving such medical interventions. Having said that, a
research/clinical  trial  participant  must  not  be  under  any
“therapeutic  misconception”,  i.e.  a  misconception  by
participants  believing  that  the  purpose  of  clinical
trials/research  is  to  administer  treatment  rather  than  to
conduct research, and therefore potential participants should
be mindful of the same.
7. At the same time, we consider it necessary to clarify that our
judgment & order dated 30.01.2026 does not foreclose the
possibility  of  such  an  intervention  being  considered
permissible in the future. The prohibition on administering
stem cell ‘therapy’ for ASD as a clinical service is founded
upon  the  state  of  scientific  evidence  and  the  prevailing
regulatory framework as on date. It does not amount to an
immutable prohibition against any future development in this
field. Should further rigorous scientific research, undertaken
in  a  duly  regulated  manner  and  in  accordance  with  the
applicable  scientific  and  ethical  standards,  establish  the
safety,  efficacy  and  ethical  acceptability  of  such  an
intervention,  the  competent  regulatory  authorities  would

--- Page 121 ---
4
remain at liberty to consider whether, and subject to what
conditions and safeguards, it may be permitted in accordance
with law.
8. Now, we turn to the compliance affidavit dated 28.09.2026,
which has been filed on behalf of the Union of India, duly
affirmed by Dr. Tushar Karmarkar, Deputy Secretary to the
Government  of  India,  Department  of  Health  Research,
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.
9. The compliance affidavit dated 28.09.2026 refers to the Office
Order No. M-11019/5/2026-CG dated 24.03.2026, issued by
the Department of Health Research, vide which the National
Stem Cell Research Regulation Committee (“NSRC”) been
constituted to oversee and regulate research on stem cells that
have undergone minimal or less than minimal manipulation.
The NSRC comprises representatives of the Department of
Biotechnology, the Department of Health and Family Welfare,
CDSCO, and the Chairman NMC (not below the rank of Joint
Secretary),  seven  permanent  experts,  along  with  subject
experts  drawn  on  rotation  from  13  specialities  as  per
requirement, and an ICMR-DHR Secretariat.
10. The Union has also submitted that the following documents
have been issued in furtherance of our judgment & order
dated 30.01.2026, in order to widely disseminate and enforce
the  regulatory  framework  governing  stem  cell  research  in
ASD:
i.  D.O. Letter No. M-11019/5/2026-CG dated 10.03.2026,
issued by the Secretary DHR & to the Chairman, NMC

--- Page 122 ---
5
ii. Advisory  No.  CDN-20011/105/2026-COORDINATION-
NMC dated 25.03.2026 issued by the National Medical
Commission
iii. Advisory  No.  R-13014/28/2022-  Ethics  dated
05.09.2026, issued by the Ethics & Medical Registration
Board, National Medical Commission
iv. Advisory  No.  C.18018/13/2026-MS  dated  16.09.2026,
issued by the Department of Health & Family Welfare,
Ministry  of  Health  &  Family  Welfare,  Government  of
India, to the Chief Secretary/Additional Chief Secretary
(Health)/Principal  Secretary  (Health),  Secretary
(Health)/Director General of Health Services/Director of
Medical Education/Nodal Officer, Clinical Establishments
(All  States/UTs  who  have  adopted  the  Clinical
Establishment Act, 2010)
11.  In response to our query that “ Whether, subsequent to the
Judgment, the competent regulatory authority has received any
application  for  approval  or  permission  to  conduct
research/clinical trial involving stem cell therapy for ASD?” , it
has been submitted that the competent regulatory authority
for stem cell research depends upon the level of manipulation
of the stem cells, as defined by the Central Drugs Standard
Control  (“CDSCO”).  Where  the  stem  cells  have  undergone
more than minimal manipulation, the research is regulated by
CDSCO under the New Drugs and Clinical Trial Rules, 2019
(“NDCT Rules, 2019 ”). Where the stem cells have undergone
minimal or less than minimal manipulation, the research is

--- Page 123 ---
6
regulated by the DHR, and in addition to the recommendation
of  the  Institutional  Ethics  Committee  registered  with  the
DHR, the trial is required to be approved by the NSRC. It was
submitted that neither the CDSCO, nor the DHR or the ICMR
have received any application seeking approval or permission
to conduct clinical trial/research with respect to stem cell
therapy for ASD.
12. It  has  also  also  been  highlighted  that  the  Union  has
recognized the need to provide a duly regulated avenue for
patients already undergoing such therapy. Hence, a multi-
center randomized controlled trial (“ RCT”) has been proposed
to be initiated at two tertiary care sites in the country: one in
North India and one in South India, within a period of six
months with funding support from the ICMR. 
13. On perusal of the compliance affidavit dated 28.09.2026, we
find  that,  although  the  Union  proposes  to  undertake
consolidation of the existing rules, regulations and guidelines
through appropriate amendments, the need of the hour is to
clearly explain the existing regulatory framework applicable to
research/clinical  trial  corresponding  to  different  levels  of
manipulation of stem cells for ASD. There is an urgent need
for a step-wise procedure to be widely disseminated amongst
the public, so as to ensure ready access to all stakeholders
involved. 
14. The  failure  of  the  authorities  to  effectively  curb  the
malpractice  of  illegally  administering  a  prohibited  form  of
medical  intervention  as  a  clinical  service  has  led  to  the

--- Page 124 ---
7
proliferation of clinics and doctors offering such services. The
lack of readily accessible information, which the public could
consult to ascertain the legal position, has tacitly enabled
such  malpractice  to  continue.  The  labyrinth  of  rules,
regulations, office orders and advisories, unless presented in
a  clear  and  coherent  manner,  leaves  room  for  such
malpractices  to  persist  and  enables  dubious  elements  to
exploit the lack of public awareness in this regard. In other
words, even though the administration of stem cell therapy for
ASD has never been permissible as a clinical service outside
an approved and monitored research or clinical trial setting,
the absence of a clear and accessible protocol has made it
easier for such interventions to be offered under the guise of
legitimate medical treatment.
15. Therefore, we hereby direct that the Ministry of Health and
Family  Welfare,  Government  of  India  to  undertake  the
following steps, within a period of 6 weeks  from the date of
this order:
i. Issue  a  comprehensive  protocol clearly  explaining  the
regulatory  regime  governing  the  use  of  stem  cells  in
research and clinical trials relating to ASD. The protocol
shall set out, in a step-wise manner, the procedure for
seeking  the  requisite  permissions  and  approvals,  the
timelines applicable at each stage, and the duties and
obligations of all stakeholders concerned. The statutory
or regulatory basis for  each step of compliance, along
with the competent authority responsible for granting the
requisite  approval  or  authorisation,  shall  be  clearly

--- Page 125 ---
8
identified and explained. Wherever practicable, it shall be
supplemented  by  a  flowchart  enabling  medical
practitioners, institutions and members of the public to
readily identify the regulatory pathway applicable to the
proposed intervention. The objective is to ensure that no
stakeholder is left to navigate a labyrinth of regulatory
instruments without being able to ascertain the precise
requirements applicable to them.
ii.  Create  awareness  and  undertake  widespread
dissemination  of  information  regarding  the  existing
regulatory framework, clearly informing the public that
stem cell therapy for ASD is not permissible as a clinical
service outside a duly approved and monitored research
or clinical trial setting. For this purpose, the Ministry
shall ensure: 
a)  That such information is published in a dedicated
and easily identifiable section of its official website,
in  clear  and  accessible  language,  and  is
disseminated  through  the  websites  of  other
relevant regulatory authorities, including the DBT,
the ICMR, the CDSCO and the NMC. 
b) That the information reaches the public at large,
particularly parents, guardians and caregivers of
persons  with  ASD,  through  hospitals,  medical
institutions, professional medical associations and
patient  support  organisations.  The  information

--- Page 126 ---
9
shall clearly distinguish between established forms
of  treatment  and  experimental  interventions,
explain  the  legal  restrictions  governing  the
administration of stem cell therapy for ASD, and
caution  the  public  against  misleading  claims
regarding its safety, efficacy or regulatory approval.
16. With respect to the Union’s proposal to initiate multicentre
Randomised Controlled Trial (“ RCT”) across the two tertiary
care  sites  indicated  in  the  compliance  affidavit,  certain
concerns  arise  regarding  the  eligibility  criteria  for
participation in such research/clinical trials. Accordingly, the
Union is directed to clarify, on the next date of hearing, the
eligibility criteria proposed to be adopted for participation in
the  RCT  and,  in  particular,  whether  the  process  of
randomisation  may  result  in  some  participants,  including
those who are already undergoing the therapy, being excluded
from the intervention under study and, consequently, being
unable to avail of its potential benefits. In the event that the
proposed  design  of  the  RCT  may  result  in  some  eligible
participants, including those already undergoing the therapy,
being excluded from receiving the intervention under study,
the Union shall deliberate upon and place before this Court a
comprehensive plan for the continued monitoring and medical
supervision of such participants, including appropriate follow-
up, assessment of their clinical condition and such further
measures as may be necessary to safeguard their health and
well-being,  in  accordance  with  applicable  scientific,  ethical

--- Page 127 ---
10
and regulatory standards.
17.  Having regard to the concerns raised and the lack of clarity,
at this stage, regarding the eligibility criteria for participation
in the proposed RCT and the precise manner in which the two
tertiary care centres are to function, we permit Respondent
No. 13 and any other interested individual to place their views
and  suggestions  before  the  National  Stem  Cell  Research
Regulation Committee for their due consideration. We direct
the  Union  to  establish  a  dedicated  online  portal  for  the
submission of such views and suggestions within a period of
4  weeks .  The  Committee  shall  duly  consider  the
representations so received, afford an opportunity of hearing
to  the  persons  concerned  wherever  necessary,  and  take
appropriate decisions in accordance with law.
18. As regards patients who had already commenced stem cell
therapy for ASD on or before 30.01.2026, we direct the Union
to  establish  a  dedicated  online  portal  for  maintaining  the
medical records of such patients, including the particulars of
the treating medical practitioners, the nature and course of
the intervention administered, and such other clinical details
as may be prescribed by the competent authority, subject to
appropriate safeguards for the confidentiality and security of
the patients’ medical information. Such online portal is to be
created within a period 6 weeks  from the date of this order.
Once the portal is established, it shall be mandatory for the
patient  or  their  parent/guardian/caregiver  and  the
doctor/clinic  administering  such  therapy,  to  register

--- Page 128 ---
11
themselves on the portal with the requisite information before
continuing with the intervention.
19. Pending the operationalisation of the proposed tertiary care
centres, patients who had commenced stem cell therapy for
ASD on or before 30.01.2026 may, as a strictly temporary
arrangement,  continue  with  the  ongoing  procedure  at  the
existing clinics or institutions, subject to their registration on
the aforesaid portal and compliance with such monitoring,
reporting and other safeguards as may be prescribed by the
competent authority. This arrangement shall be confined to
existing patients and shall not be construed as recognition or
approval of stem cell therapy for ASD as a permissible clinical
service. 
20. We reiterate that no new patients shall be inducted for stem
cell therapy for ASD outside a duly approved and monitored
research or clinical trial setting. The temporary arrangement
set out above is confined to patients who had commenced
such  therapy  on  or  before  30.01.2026  and  shall  not  be
construed as diluting the regulatory position clarified in the
judgment dated 30.01.2026.
21. Registry shall furnish one copy of this Order to Ms. Aishwarya
Bhati, the learned ASG for its onward communication.

p.m.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. We have perused the compliance affidavit of the State of Karnataka and it is
indicated in Paragraph No.8 to the following effect :
 
“8. Presently, in continuation of the averments made in the above
affidavit,  the  requisite  information  has  been  received  from  the
Department  of  Survey,  Settlement  and  Land  Records  GoK,  on
25.09.2026  through  e-mail.  The  details  furnished  by  the  said
Department  are  reproduced  below  for  kind  consideration  of  the
Hon’ble Court.”
Sl. 
No.
Description Number of 
Wetlands
1. T otal Wetlands in Karnataka
(MoEFCC data)
14, 936
2. Wetlands ground-truthed 14, 355
3. Wetlands surveyed with boundary 
demarcation data available
14, 355
2. The mode, manner and method in which the said ground truthing has been
done as well as procedure adopted along with supporting documents in respect
of the ground truthing carried out together the manner in which demarcation
has been made is not accompanying the compliance affidavit dated 25.09.2026.
Hence, we direct the State of Karnataka to place on record all these documents
within four (4) weeks from today. 
9

--- Page 142 ---
3. This Court by order dated 07.10.2025 had clearly observed that the ‘ground
truthing and demarcation’ of wetland boundaries is to be undertaken by each of
the  State/Union  T erritories  wetland  authorities  in  coordination  with  the
concerned nodal department as provided under the Wetlands (Conservation and
Management) Rules, 2017 (Rules, 2017). This Court also reiterated that the said
exercise which is being carried out, shall be in compliance with Rule 7(1)(a) of
the Rules, 2017. The compliance affidavits do not indicate as to whether the
exercise which has been undertaken is in compliance with Rule 7(1)(a) of the
Rules, 2017.
4.  It  would  be  profitable  to  note  that State  of  T amil  Nadu seems  to  have
undertaken the aforesaid exercise and the systematic manner in which the said
exercise has been undertaken, has been narrated in the note supplied to this
Court  today  by  Shri  Shekhar  Naphade,  learned  Senior  Counsel,  during  the
course of his arguments/submissions. For the purpose of convenience we set
out the same hereinbelow:
“A. TIME TAKEN PER WATERBODY-SHAPEFILE
4. At the outset the State of Tamil Nadu submits that it respects
and abides by the orders of this Hon'ble Court and apologises for
the non-completion of the entire boundary demarcation process
as directed. It is submitted that this failure is inadvertent and
despite  the  bona  fide  best  efforts  to  complete  the  task .  With
28,898 waterbodies/shapefiles to complete, the State of Tamil Nadu
has the largest task to execute.
5.  The  exercise  requires  substantial  human  resources,  logistical
arrangements and financial expenditure, with coordinated action by the
Revenue,  Forest,  Rural  Development  and  Water  Resources
Departments. The time taken to complete each step of the process per
waterbody/shapefile ranges  from a minimum of 1-2 days to 10-15
days  depending  upon  the  area,  location  of  the  waterbody  and
other factors. The State of Tamil Nadu is committed to completing the
task in an expedient manner.
B. TRANSLATION OF SATELLITE IMAGES INTO ISRO
SHAPEFILES
6.  Pursuant  to  the  Orders  of  this  Hon'ble  Court,  the  MoEF  &  CC
communicated  the  shapefiles  of  the  National  Wetland  Inventory
10

--- Page 143 ---
Assessment (NWIA) 2011 and the National Wetlands Decadal Change
Atlas (NWDCA) 2021, prepared by ISRO's Space Application Centre
(SAC),  Ahmedabad.  The  shapefiles  corresponding  to  28,898
waterbodies in Tamil Nadu were extracted therefrom, making this the
largest such exercise among all the States in the country.
7. Methodology for generation of shapefiles : ISRO's LISS-III sensor
captures the Earth's surface as a grid of 23.5m × 23.5m pixels. Since
water absorbs nearly all Near-Infrared and Shortwave-Infrared (SWIR)
radiation  while  land  and  vegetation  reflect  it,  ISRO  computes  the
Modified Normalized Difference Water Index (MNDWI) for every pixel,
classifies each pixel as "Water" or "Non-Water", and traces the outer
edges of contiguous water pixels into vector polygons packaged as
ESRI Shapefiles. These polygons thus represent only the water-spread
visible at the moment of the satellite pass.
8. Such shapefiles, by themselves, cannot establish precise cadastral
or legal boundaries on the ground, because:
(i) LISS-III maps operate at a 1:50,000 scale where 1 mm equals 50
meters on the ground;
(ii) Mosaicking of 365 orbital scenes causes systematic spatial shifts of
20-100m,  documented  across  7  districts  (Kanniyakumari,  Tenkasi,
Tirunelveli,  Thoothukudi,  Nilgiris,  Virudhunagar,  Coimbatore)
(Annexure  R-21  in  Compliance  Affidavit  dated  26.09.2026  @pg.
106); and
(iii) Satellites measure instantaneous water reflectance and cannot see
survey  numbers,  FMB  sketches,  A-Registers  or  Patta  titles.  The
polygons must therefore be superimposed on village cadastral maps
and  verified  against  revenue  records  before  boundaries  can  be
physically demarcated.
C. MARKING OF BOUNDARIES FROM ISRO SHAPEFILES
9.  To  convert  satellite  shapefiles  into  legal  boundaries,  the  State
executes a 4-stage workflow:
 Stage  1  (Mobile  GIS  Ground  Truthing) :  Teams  use  centroid
coordinates  to  visit  sites  with  ArcGIS  Survey123  app,  uploading
geotagged GPS photos ( Compliance Affidavit dated 26.09.2026 @
pgs. 101-103);
 Stage 2 (Digital Boundary Delineation ): GIS experts superimpose
satellite polygons on village cadastral maps (TNeGA/TNGIS) within a
300m buffer zone;
 Stage  3  (Revenue  Record  Reconciliation ):  Tahsildars  examine
cadastral maps, FMB  sketches, A-Register extracts, Adangal, and
Patta titles, fixing the wetland boundary as the outer envelope of
maximum normal monsoon inundation (15+ days submerged);
 Stage 4 (Survey & Pillar Installation ): Surveyors deploy Differential
GPS (DGPS) equipment or any available survey method to extract
11

--- Page 144 ---
coordinates and erect boundary stones/pillars (at corners, bends, 50-
200m  intervals),  logging  entries  in  Boundary  Stone  Register.
(Compliance Affidavit dated 26.09.2026 @ pgs. 104, 110-176).
STAGE 1 COMPLIANCE
10.Field  officers  visit  the  coordinates  provided  by  the  ISRO  SAC
shapefiles using the 'ArcGIS  Survey 123' mobile app developed by
NCSCM, verify the existence of the waterbody and upload geotagged
photographs ( Annexure R-20 in Compliance Affidavit @ pgs. 101-
103).  The  ground  truthing  is  100%  complete  for  all  28,898
waterbodies/shapefiles.
STAGE 2 COMPLIANCE
11.GIS specialists at TNSWA and Tamil Nadu e-Governance Agency
(TNeGA) superimpose the ISRO SAC shapefiles onto digitised village
cadastral maps and extract all revenue survey numbers within a 300-
metre envelope of each polygon. This step is mandatory to correct the
resolution, spatial-shift and seasonal reflectance inaccuracies inherent
in satellite data. It has been COMPLETED in  26/38 Districts (15,029
waterbodies authenticated) and is actively being done in the remaining
12/38 Districts (13,869 waterbodies).
STAGE 3 COMPLIANCE
12.Stages  3  and  4  are  carried  out  through  a  four-tier  set  up:  the
TNSWA (chaired by the Hon'ble Forest Minister and vice-chaired by the
Chief  Secretary);  its  Member  Secretary;  District  Level  Wetlands
Management Committees chaired by the District Collectors; and Joint
Field  Inspection  Teams  (Tahsildars,  VAOs,  Surveyors,  BDOS,  WRD
Engineers).  These  officers  hold  ex-officio  appointments  while
discharging their regular statutory duties (monsoon flood relief, disaster
management, law and order, revenue collection, election duties), which
imposes severe operational constraints that are being tackled by the
officers.
13.  The  present  status  of  Revenue  survey  number  verification  is
:COMPLETED  in  16/38  Districts  (9,202  waterbodies  authenticated)
Active in 22/38 Districts (19,696 waterbodies)
STAGE 4 COMPLIANCE
14. Physical boundary demarcation entails field surveying (using DGPS
wherever available) and installation of boundary stones/pillars at every
corner,  change  of  direction  and  road/canal  crossing,  at  100-200m
intervals on straight stretches and 50-100m on curves ( Annexure R-18
in Compliance Affidavit @ pg. 81). Currently, 3,113 physical boundary
stones/pillars  have  been  erected,  geotagged  and  authenticated  on
12

--- Page 145 ---
ground (surging from 290 on 18.09.2026 and 2,614 on 26.09.2026).
15.The  time  required  varies  with  the  extent  and  perimeter  of  each
waterbody,  availability  of  revenue  records,  terrain,  accessibility,
vegetation  and  weather.  Tamil  Nadu  has  the  largest  number  of
wetlands in India, and complex historical revenue record matching and
monsoon inundation further constrain surveying and pillar installation.
Numbering, painting and logging of each stone/pillar in the Boundary
Stone  Register  and  preparation  of  KML files  is  planned  across  all
districts.”
5. A perusal of the above steps taken, would indicate that it seems to be in a
systematic  and  scientific manner  the  exercise  of  ground  truthing  has  been
undertaken. Hence, we direct all the States to undertake the same and similar
exercise, if not already undertaken, which shall also be in compliance with Rule
7(1)  of  the  Rules, 2017 indicated hereinabove,  expeditiously  and on a war
footing basis. The water bodies being source of drinking water is precious and
would encompass within the four corners of right to live, as guaranteed under
the Constitution of India. T his Court cannot remain as a mere spectator or be
unmindful  of  the  consequences  flowing  from  water  bodies  remaining
unprotected. In order to achieve this avowed object, we have issued directions
to  the  States  and  Wetland Authorities  to  undertake  the  exercise  of  ground
truthing (physically) and we reiterate the same and direct that all the States /
Wetland Authorities should undertake the said exercise forthwith as undertaken
by the State of T amil Nadu, if not already undertaken, and file a compliance
affidavit indicating thereunder the mode and method in which the exercise has
been undertaken. The said affidavit by the respective States shall be filed within
an outer limit of four weeks from tod ay. Shri Naphade, learned Senior Counsel
has vociferously contended that undertaking the exercise of ground truthing by
the officials would be time-consuming exercise and has prayed for reasonable
time of six to nine months being granted. This Court is fully conscious of the
enormous  physical  work  that  would  be  involved,  apart  from  coordination
between departments. Yet, being alive to the situation, we deem it proper to
grant four months' time to complete the said exercise.
13

--- Page 146 ---
6. We  also  hasten  to  add the  exercise  of  ground truthing which has  been
referred to hereinabove relates to wetlands, would also include the other water
bodies, viz., other than the wetlands. Same shall also be identified, specified,
indicated and marked in the Report and we reiterate what has been indicated in
Paragraph No.8 of our order dated 19.08.2025 and for immediate reference and
for the convenience, the same is extracted hereinbelow :
“8. The statistics furnished today would also reflect that wetlands

which according to the statistics is around 5,55,557 as mentioned
in the Wetland Atlas.”
7.  It would be of benefit to note that Rule 7(1)(a) of the Rules, 2017 (supra)
clearly mandates that the concerned department of the State Government or
Union T erritory Administration shall within a period of one year from the date of
publication of the Rules, prepare a brief document for each of the wetland
identified for notification providing details envisaged under clause (a) to (g) of
Rule 7(1) of the Rules, 2017 which has not been undertaken by the States. It is
for  this  precise  reason  the  directions  and  orders  came  to  be  passed  on
11.12.2024, 19.08.2025, 07.10.2025, 28.10.2025 and 28.07.2026. Even after
nine years from the date of publication of Rules, this exercise is not completed
or concluded. As such, the directions have been issued and for appropriate
further direction being issued in respect of each of the States, we call upon all
the States to file the affidavit indicated hereinabove within an outer limit of four
weeks from today indicating the status of ground truthing being done including
other water bodies.
8.  The affidavits directed to be filed by the States, shall be furnished to the
Nodal Counsel for compiling the same and being filed.

IA No.103382/2025
1. This application is filed for appointment of a valuer to value the cost involved
in restoring the T emple T anks of India.
2. We have heard Mr. M K Balakrishnan, party appearing in person. It is his
contention that there are more than 100 kunds (big tanks) in Vrindavan, out of
which 80% are in dilapidated condition. Hence, it is contended that a direction
be issued to the authorities to entrust the work of restoration of these temple
tanks  to  the  intervener,  National  NGO  wedded  to  the  protection  of  Indian
Wetlands and therefore to appoint a valuer for valuing the cost involved in
restoring these dilapidated kunds in perfect condition. 
3. This Court while examining prayer sought for in IA No.76117/2025 by order
dated 28.07.2026 had rejected the application qua a direction sought for to the
Union of India to pay a sum of Rs.80 crores for undertaking the restoration of
more than 100 kunds situated in Vrindavan. This Court also observed that the
water bodies in the entire country having been identified by SAC Atlas vests
with the wetland authority of the States and or different instrumentalities of the
States and appropriate directions to the State and its instrumentalities, would
be issued on receipt of the Report that has been called for. Hence, we have
rejected the prayer sought for in IA 76117/2025.
4. In view of the same, question of appointing a valuer, at this stage, that too
for ascertaining the condition of the tanks, does not arise. IA No.103382/2025
stands rejected.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NOS.8437-8438/2013
ASSET RECONSTRUCTION COMPANY (INDIA) LTD        Appellant(s)
      VERSUS
THE STATE OF GUJARAT & ORS.                     Respondent(s)
                            
WITH
CIVIL APPEAL NO.8439/2013 (III-B)
CIVIL APPEAL NOS.8435-8436/2013 
     O R D E R
1. We have heard the learned Senior counsel appearing
for the appellant(s) and the learned ASG appearing for
the respondent(s).
2. The  disputed  property  originally  belonged  to
Indequip Engineering Company, the appellant in Civil
Appeal No. 8439 of 2013 (hereinafter referred to as, “the
Company”). Upon the coming into force of the Urban Land
(Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976 (hereinafter referred
to as,“the Act”), the Company filed a statement under
Section 6 of the Act declaring its landholding. 
3. During the pendency of the proceedings, the Company
obtained permission to mortgage the land in favour of the
Bank of India, pursuant to which the land was mortgaged.
The Bank subsequently instituted a suit for recovery of
its dues amounting to 11.50 crores. Thereafter, the₹

--- Page 162 ---
2
Competent Authority passed an order under Section 8(4) of
the Act declaring 47,374 square metres of land as excess
vacant land. The appeals preferred by the Company and the
Bank under Section 33 of the Act were dismissed by the
Urban  Land  Tribunal  (hereinafter  referred  to  as,
“Tribunal”). 
4. Subsequently, a notification under Section 10(3)
was issued, followed by a notice under Section 10(5) for
taking  possession  of  the  excess  vacant  land.  As
possession  was  not  voluntarily  surrendered,  the
authorities claim to have taken possession by drawing a
panchanama.
5. Aggrieved by the Tribunal’s order, the Company
filed a Special Civil Application before the High Court,
wherein an order directing the parties to maintain status
quo was passed. During the pendency of the proceedings,
the Receiver appointed in the Bank’s recovery suit was
impleaded  as  petitioner  No.2  in  the  Special  Civil
Application.
6. The  Special  Civil  Application  was  ultimately
dismissed by the Learned Single Judge. Challenging the
said judgment, the Receiver and the Bank filed intra-
court appeals. During the pendency of the appeals, the
Bank  assigned  its  rights  in  favour  of  Asset
Reconstruction Company, the appellant in the main Civil
Appeal  (hereinafter  referred  to  as,  “the  main

--- Page 163 ---
3
appellant”). The main appellant was accordingly impleaded
as a respondent in the appeal. 
7. The intra-court appeals were subsequently dismissed
by  the  Division  Bench.  Aggrieved  thereby,  the  main
appellant,  the  Company  and  Mangalkrupa  Cooperative
Housing  Society,  the  highest  bidder  in  the  auction
conducted by the Bank, are before us in Civil Appeal Nos.
8437-38/2013, 8439/2013 and 8435-8436/2013, respectively.
8. The  learned  Senior  Counsel  appearing  for  the
appellant(s) raised the following submissions:
a) The possession of the land in question has not been
taken. The respondent has failed to prove the factum of
taking possession, as mandated under law.  There has been
no due compliance with Section 10(6) of the Act. The
materials on record, including the proceedings before the
Civil Court, indicates that the possession continued to
remain with the Court Receiver.
b) The Panchnama also does not indicate the factum of
taking possession.  In support of his contention, learned
Senior counsel relied upon the following judgments:
(i) Dalsukhbhai Bachhubhai v. State of Gujarat – 2026 SCC
OnLine 25;
(ii) AP Electrical Equipment Corp. v. Tehsildar –  2025
SCC OnLine 447;
(iii) Gajanan Kamlya Patil v. Addl. Collector & Competent
Authority – (2014) 12 SCC 523;
(iv) State U.P. v. Hari Ram (2013) 4 SCC 280;

--- Page 164 ---
4
(v) Avanti Organisation, Rajkot v. Additional Collector &
Competent Authority, Urban Land Ceiling, Rajkot  – 1988
SCC OnLine Guj 107;
(vi) Katya Co-Operative Building Society Limited & Ors.
v. The Government of Andhra Pradesh – AIR 1985 AP 242.
9. Learned counsel appearing for the respondent(s) on
the other hand would submit that the appeals are not
maintainable on two grounds. Firstly, the main appellant
before us can, at best, claim the status of a mortgagee,
being an assignee of the Bank, who was the mortgagee. The
fact that permission had earlier been granted by the
authorities to create  the mortgage does not enure to the
benefit  of  the  main  appellant.  Secondly,  the  legal
possession of the excess vacant land was duly taken. The
record  pertaining  to  the  building  situated  on  the
disputed land was prepared subsequently and was illegal.
In  any  event,  that  would  not  render  the  Panchnama
invalid, as under the Act, only possession of the excess
vacant land is required to be taken. It was further
submitted  that  there  is  no  requirement  to  issue  a
separate notice under Section 10(6) of the Act, as the
notice issued under Section 10(5) of the Act itself
clearly indicates the consequence of failure to surrender
the possession of the land to the Government or any
person authorised by the Government. 
10. The learned Counsel appearing for the Respondent
also submitted that the earlier proceedings under Section

--- Page 165 ---
5
33 of the Act would operate as res judicata against the
Bank, the predecessor-in-interest of the main appellant,
since it did not prefer any appeal against the order
passed by the Tribunal. It was, therefore, contended that
no interference is warranted, particularly when both the
Courts have concurrently held against the appellant(s).
It was further submitted that the main appellant had not
independently challenged the Tribunal’s order and was
impleaded only as a respondent in the Special Civil
Application filed by the Company, the erstwhile land
owner, which itself  chose not to file any intra-Court
appeal before the High Court.
11. On  perusal  of  the  records  and  the  statutory
provisions, we are not inclined to hold that section
10(6) of the Act,  per se , mandates the issuance of a
separate notice. We have also perused the notice under
Section 10(5) of the Act, which is a comprehensive
notice. This notice clearly stipulates the requirement of
handing over possession and the consequences that would
follow in the event of failure to surrender possession.
The finding on record is that the said notice was duly
served.  As  stated  Section  10(6)  of  the  Act  only
facilitates the Urban Land Ceiling Authority to take
possession in the event of non-compliance with the notice
issued under Section 10(5) of the Act.  It does not
mandate the issuance of a fresh notice before action is
taken under Section 10(6) of the Act. In other words, the

--- Page 166 ---
6
statutory scheme primarily contemplates the taking over
of possession of the excess vacant land, which, according
to the record, has been done in the present case.
12. There is no difficulty in holding that it is for
the authorities to satisfy the Court that, pursuant to
the Panchnama drawn, the possession has been taken.
However, we are inclined to hold that the right of the
main  appellant  is  rather  restricted  in  nature.
Furthermore,  the  main  appellant’s  predecessor-in-
interest,namely, the Bank, did not file the Special Civil
Application challenging the order passed by the Tribunal
and was only arrayed as a respondent in the Special Civil
Application filed by the Company. The Company, in turn,
did not file the intra-court appeal against the judgment
of the learned Single Judge dismissing the Special Civil
Application. The learned Single Judge has specifically
noted that the Company had abandoned the litigation and
had shown no active interest in pursuing it. Thereafter,
the Company chose to file the present appeal directly
before us. However, none has appeared on its behalf. We
have  also  been  informed  that  the  Company  is  under
liquidation. Perhaps that is the reason why it has chosen
not to pursue the present litigation before us.
13. Merely because permission was granted to create the
mortgage does not enure to the benefits of the main
appellant. In other words, what the main appellant seeks
before us is an order extending to it the benefits

--- Page 167 ---
7
available under Sections 3 and 4 of the Act. It is for the
Company, the erstwhile landowner, to make such a claim.
The proceedings before the Civil Court, to which the
respondent(s) are not parties, would not enure to the
benefit of the main appellant. As stated earlier, we are
concerned only with the possession of the excess vacant
land.
14. The other contention regarding the panchnama also
does not hold good, as it is for the Company, the
erstwhile  landowner,  to  raise  the  appropriate  plea.
Having found that the notice issued under Section 10(5)
of the Act was duly served, and that it clearly indicated
the consequential action that would follow upon failure
to surrender possession of the land, it is too late in
the day to permit the main appellant to raise all such
contentions on merits before us. Suffice it to state that
the main appellant is merely an assignee of the erstwhile
Bank, in whose favour the property in question had been
mortgaged.
15. Accordingly, we are inclined to hold that the
judgments relied upon by the learned counsel appearing
for the appellant(s), in our considered view, do not have
any bearing on the facts of the case.
16. Taking  note  of  the  facts  and  circumstances
governing the case, we have no hesitation in holding that
the order passed by the Division Bench under challenge
deserves to be affirmed, particularly when no intra-court

--- Page 168 ---
8
appeal was filed by the Company, the erstwhile landowner.
The main appellant before us also did not choose to
challenge the proceedings by filing a Special Civil
Application; instead, it preferred an intra-court appeal
against the order passed in the Special Civil Application
filed by the Company. Additionally, we take note of the
fact  that  the  predecessor-in-interest  of  the  main
appellant had invoked Section 33 of the Act, whereupon
the  Tribunal  held  that  it  had  no  locus  standi to
challenge the proceedings. The said order has attained
finality as against the predecessor of the main appellant
and is, therefore, binding upon the main appellant. In
other words, the main appellant continues to be merely a
mortgagee and, therefore, its rights are circumscribed by
the law governing mortgage alone.
17. We are conscious of the fact that we are dealing with
a very hard case. As recorded by us, there was an element
of lack of due diligence on the part of the predecessor
of the main appellant in obtaining prior permission from
the authorities before executing the deed of mortgage.
Apart from the substantial dues payable to the main
appellant, we are also confronted with the competing
interests of the erstwhile employees.
18. In such view of the matter, we grant liberty to the
main appellant, the Company, its erstwhile employees
including respondent No.8 in Civil Appeal No.8439/2013,
Rashtriya Majdoor Sangh to make a representation to

--- Page 169 ---
9
respondent No.1-State, seeking release of the specific
portion of the land declared as surplus, which may
include the constructed portion as well.
19.  We make it clear that we have not expressed any
opinion on the subsequent action of the Bank in bringing
the property to sale, as the same gives rise to a
separate cause of action.
20.  Accordingly, the appeals stand dismissed.  No costs.
21.   Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

1. Leave granted.
2. I.A.  No.314784/2026  filed  by  Respondent  No.2  to
appear and argue in person, for which two weeks’ time is
sought for, is rejected.

Respondent  No.1-State  of  Jharkhand;  and  Ms.  Mrigna
1

Shekhar, learned counsel for Respondent No.2-complainant.
4. Appellant is aggrieved by order dated 24.08.2026
passed by the High Court of Jharkhand at Ranchi (briefly
the ‘High Court’ hereinafter), rejecting the regular bail
application of the appellant (B.A. No.7139/2026).
5. Appellant is an accused in FIR No.280/2025 registered
at Police Station- Bank More, District- Dhanbad, Jharkhand
under Sections 111(2)(b), 316(2), 316(5), 318(4), 338,
336(3), 340(2), 61(2) and 3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya
Sanhita, 2023 (for short, ‘BNS’).
6. Allegation against the appellant is that the company,
M/s. Vimla Fuels & Metals Limited, of which he is the
Director,  had  entered  into  certain  transactions  with
Respondent No.2. For the amount received by the company
from Respondent No.2, certain parcels of land were offered
as surety to Respondent No.2. It is the allegation of
Respondent No.2 that neither the amount taken by the
appellant has been returned nor the lands offered as
surety could be utilized for recovery as one parcel of
land was found to be sold to the wife of Accused No.1
(Sanjay Kumar Agarwal); while the title of another plot of
land was under a cloud.
7. Appellant was arrested on 02.04.2026 and has been in
custody since then.
8. Mr.  Shoeb  Alam,  learned  Senior  counsel  for  the
appellant submits that altogether 04 plots of land were
offered as surety to Respondent No.2. While there can be
2

--- Page 176 ---
an issue with one plot of land, the other 03 plots of land
have clear title and available with Respondent No.2 to
realize the outstanding dues. His further submission is
that  it  is  a  purely  commercial  dispute  between  the
appellant and Respondent No.2, who has misused the various
provisions of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023
(for  short,  ‘BNSS’),  more  particularly  Section  111
thereof,  to  implicate  the  appellant  in  criminal
proceedings.
9. Learned  counsel  for  Respondent  No.1-State  of
Jharkhand submits that appellant is involved in similar
kinds of dubious transactions in Gujarat as well as in
West Bengal. It is for this reason that Section 111 of the
BNSS has been invoked against the appellant. That apart,
appellant has 04 criminal antecedents of similar nature.
10. On  a  query  by  the  Court,  he  submits  that
investigation is complete, whereafter charge-sheet was
submitted before the Trial Court. Matter is at the stage
of framing of charges.
11. Learned  counsel  for  Respondent  No.2-complainant,
while adopting the submissions of learned counsel for
Respondent No.1-State of Jharkhand, submits that it is the
modus operandi  of the appellant to indulge in similar
kinds of transactions which has taken place in Gujarat,
West Bengal and now in the State of Jharkhand. As a result
of the fraudulent activity of the appellant, Respondent
No.2 had to run from pillar to post for recovery of his
3

--- Page 177 ---
own money. Her further submission is that appellant had
deliberately offered as surety a plot of land, knowing
fully well that the same was sold to another person, who
happens to be the wife of another accused. Additionally,
there is a cloud over the title of the 2 nd property.
Considering the criminal antecedents of the appellant and
the huge amount of money which has been duped from
Respondent  No.2,  Court  may  not  grant  bail  to  the
appellant. She further submits that the trial could not
commence because of the conduct of the appellant himself,
who did not furnish bail bond before the Gujarat Court for
which he is languishing in jail in Gujarat, as a result he

is the reason for the delay in the trial.
12. Submissions made by learned counsel for the parties
have received the due consideration of the Court.
13. First and the foremost, we find that the allegation
of Respondent No.2 pertains to fraudulent transactions of
money  and  property  between  Respondent  No.2  and  the
appellant. There is no allegation that appellant has
defrauded the revenue of the State. Further, we find that
investigation is complete whereafter charge-sheet has been
filed. Matter is now pending before the Trial Court.
Insofar the 04 criminal antecedents are concerned, we find
that in the Gandhidham P.S. case (Gujarat), appellant has

at Kolkata, West Bengal, interim protection has been
4

--- Page 178 ---
granted by this Court on 14.10.2026 (matter is pending
before this Court); the 3 rd case is again at Gujarat in

Sessions Court at Ahmedabad; in the 4 th case which is at
Dhanbad, Jharkhand, appellant has been granted bail by the
Jharkhand High Court on 10.06.2026. We also find that M/s
Narayani Coke Private Limited, of which Respondent No.2 is
the authorized signatory, as the Operational Creditor has
intervened in the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process
of  M/s  Vimla  Fuels  &  Metals  Limited,  of  which  the

Tribunal at Ahmedabad in CP(IB) 201/2025.

grant bail to the appellant.

1. The present petition calls in question the correctness of
the order 09-10-2026 in WP No. 3102/2026 passed by the High
Court of Judicature at Bombay. By the said order, the High
Court has made the following operative directions pending the

“20.  In  the  meanwhile,  in  the  light  of  the
observations  made  hereinabove,  respondent  No.  6,
Bankruptcy Trustee, is directed to hand over physical
possession of the subject property to the petitioner
on or before 12.10.2026.
21. This Court will not tolerate any obstruction
created by any of the respondents with regard to
execution of the said direction, including respondent
No. 4 or any third party.
22.  It  is  further  directed  that  upon  taking
possession, the petitioner, shall not create third-
party rights in the subject property, until further
orders,  as  this  would  create  unnecessary

--- Page 188 ---
3

23. Needless to say, the handing over of possession to
the petitioner would be subject to further orders in
this writ petition and subject to the final result
thereof.
24.  It  is  further  clarified  that  upon  taking
possession of the subject property, the petitioner
would be entitled to undertake minor repairs in the
property, but no structural or major modifications
shall be undertaken.
25. Since the petitioner is being restrained from
dealing  with  the  subject  property  after  taking
possession thereof, it would be only in the fitness of

Ordered accordingly.”

3. Heard Mr. Shyam Divan, learned Senior Counsel for the

--- Page 191 ---
6
Bankruptcy Trustee, who is the petitioner;  Mr. S. Niranjan
Reddy,  learned  Senior  Counsel  for  some  of  the  creditors
supporting the Bankruptcy Trustee,  Mr. Maninder Singh, learned
Senior  Counsel  appearing  on  caveat  for  respondent  no.1-
purchaser of the property by a private treaty, Mr. Nakul Dewan,
learned Senior Counsel and Ms. Megha Gupta, learned counsel,
appearing for respondent nos.2 and 3-secured creditors.
4. Mr.  Shyam  Divan,  learned  Senior  Counsel  for  the
petitioner contends that the High Court could not entertain a
writ petition when the alternate remedies were available before
the  National  Company  Law  Appellate  Tribunal  (for  short,
‘NCLAT’); that in any event on 24.04.2026, the National Company
Law Tribunal, Mumbai (for short, ‘NCLT’) had admitted the
Company Petition No.593/2025 and appointed the petitioner as a
Bankruptcy Trustee of respondent no.4. Learned Senior Counsel
further contends that the order of admission was communicated
to the petitioner on 29.04.2026.
5. Referring to Section 128 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy
Code, 2016 (for short, ‘IBC’), learned Senior Counsel contends
that on the passing of a Bankruptcy Order, the estate of a
bankrupt shall vest in the Bankruptcy Trustee as provided in
Section 154 of the IBC. Learned Senior Counsel contends that
under Section 154 of the IBC the vesting is immediately from
the date of appointment of Bankruptcy Trustee and such vesting
is  to  take  effect  without  any  conveyance,  assignment  or
transfer.
6. Mr. Shyam Divan, learned Senior Counsel further contends

--- Page 192 ---
7
that for the High Court was not justified in the teeth of the
statutory provisions, at the interim stage, to direct handing
over of the possession back to respondent no.1.
7. Mr. S. Niranjan Reddy, learned Senior Counsel supported
the learned Senior Counsel for the petitioner, by drawing
attention to Regulation 31 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy
Board of India (Bankruptcy Process for Personal Guarantors to
Corporate Debtors) Regulations, 2019 (for short, ‘IBBI’) and
contended that any secured creditor who seek to realize a
security ought to intimate the Bankruptcy Trustee of the price
at which he proposes to realize the secured asset.
8. Regulation 31 of the IBBI reads as under:-
“31. Realisation of security interest. 
(1)  A  secured  creditor,  who  seeks  to  realise  his
security, shall intimate the bankruptcy trustee of the
price at which he proposes to realise the secured asset.
(2) The bankruptcy trustee shall attempt to identify a
buyer willing to purchase the security at a price higher
than the price intimated under sub-regulation (1), and
the asset shall then be sold to such buyer, if any, at
the higher price by the secured creditor.
(3) Where the secured asset is realised under sub-
regulation (2), the cost of identification of the buyer
shall form part of bankruptcy process cost.
(4) If the bankruptcy trustee does not identify a buyer
under sub-regulation (2), or the person so identified
does not buy the secured asset, the secured creditor may
realise the secured asset in the manner it deems fit, but
at least at the price intimated under sub-regulation (1)
and shall bear the cost of identification of the buyer.
(5) Where a secured creditor realises his security and

--- Page 193 ---
8
the amount realised is in excess of the debts due to the
secured creditor, such creditor shall tender such excess
to the bankruptcy trustee.”
9. According  to  Mr.  S.  Niranjan  Reddy,  learned  Senior
Counsel, the said procedure was not complied with.
10. In response Mr. Nakul Dewan, learned Senior Counsel and
Ms. Megha Gupta, learned counsel contend that in the present
case, the sale was confirmed of the property situated in the
3rd, 4 th and 5 th Floor of the Aadhya Building, Jaihind Co-
operative Housing Society Ltd., Plot No.43, N.S.Road No.10,
Vile Parle (West), Mumbai, Maharashtra, to respondent no.1-
purchaser on 31.03.2025.
11. It  was  contended  from  payment  of  Rs.6.26  crores
approximately of the total agreed price of Rs.25.07 crores was
made. Learned Senior Counsel and learned counsel contend that
the  respondent  nos.2  &  3  had  mortgage  interest  in  the
property(es) in question and even as per the terms of the
mortgage, respondent no.1 had the right of the first refusal.
12. Learned Senior Counsel and learned counsel contend that
the proceedings were initiated under Section 13(2) of the
Securitisation  and  Reconstruction  of  Financial  Assets  and
Enforcement  of  Security  Interest  Act,  2002  (for  short,
‘SARFAESI Act’) and that multiple auction notices were not
fruitful.
13. Thereafter,  by  a  private  treaty,  the  property(ies)
was/were agreed to be sold. Learned Senior Counsel and learned

--- Page 194 ---
9
counsel contend that the respondent no.4-Bankrupt has resorted
to all steps to defeat the sale. At the last the NCLT for moved
for initiation of bankruptcy proceedings under Section 122 of
the IBC, resulting in the order of 24.04.2026, before the full
consideration could be paid by the respondent no.1. 
14. Their contention was supported by Mr. Maninder Singh,
learned Senior Counsel for purchaser-respondent no.1. Learned
Senior Counsel contended that respondent no.1, has parted with
Rs.25.07 crores pursuant to the order of the High Court dated
21.07.2026 and that the respondent no.1 is entitled to retain
possession as per the interim order.
15. We have considered the submissions of learned Senior
Counsel/Counsel appearing for the parties and perused the
records.
16. Prima facie we are of the opinion that with the vesting
of the property(ies) with the Bankruptcy Trustee under Section
128 read with 154 of the IBC on 24.04.2026, title having not
passed on to the purchaser-respondent no.1, we are of the
opinion that the High Court could not made an interim order
directing handing over of the possession of the property(ies)
in question.
17. At this stage, Mr. Maninder Singh, learned Senior Counsel
for purchaser-respondent no.1 draws attention to the amended
provisions of the Section 13(8) of the SARFAESI Act to contend
that unlike the provisions that obtained before the amendment,
the borrower loses the right of redemption upon issuance of the
first auction notice even if the auction fails. According to

--- Page 195 ---
10
learned Senior Counsel, this would mean that before the order
admitting the bankruptcy petition; appointment of Bankruptcy
Trustee, the borrower-respondent no.4 having lost the right of
redemption, the property(es) could not be set to be part of the
estate of the bankrupt.
18. This contention is seriously disputed by Mr. S.Niranjan
Reddy, learned Senior Counsel and submits that where the
purchaser had defaulted deposit of balance consideration, the
right of redemption is not lost and would always be available.
Independent of that, learned Senior Counsel submits that the
sale process could be challenged.
19. We set aside the impugned order and direct respondent
no.1 to put the petitioner in possession of the property(ies)
in question on or before 30.10.2026.
20. All  contentions  available  to  the  parties  including
contentions with regard to maintainability of the writ petition
are left open to be decided by the High Court.
21. Considering the fact that the purchaser had parted with
the  money  and  considering  that  the  claimants-  Bankruptcy
Trustee also would be eagerly awaiting for their claim to be
settled, we request the High Court to make an endevour to
dispose of the writ petition itself within a period of twelve
weeks from today.
22. Needless to say that the writ petition will be disposed
of uninfluenced by any of the observations made in the order of
the High Court or in the present order.
23. With these observations, the Special Leave Petition is

--- Page 196 ---
11
disposed of.
24. All pending applications including IA No. 321824/2026 and
IA No. 321838/2026 shall also stand disposed of.
(NIRMALA NEGI)                                  (NIKITA SINGH)

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The matter was listed today for the first time after we
delivered the final judgment. It has come up today to give
us  a  fair  idea,  how  the  Union  of  India  and  other
stakeholders  have  proceeded  to  comply  with  various
directions issued by us in the main judgment.
2. We dealt with a very delicate, rather a very important
and sensitive issue relating to the human trafficking of
women and children for commercial sexual exploitation. We,
in fact, provided an extensive ‘Victim Protection Plan’ for
strict adherence by all stakeholders in exercise of our
plenary powers under Article 142 of the Constitution. We had
also dealt with, in detail, the prayer as regards the
constitution of the Organized Crime Investigation Agency
(OCIA).  Moreover,  from  paragraphs  387  to  424,  we  had
provided certain recommendations and suggestions for serious
consideration by the Union of India.
3

--- Page 210 ---
3. Ms. Aparna Bhat, the learned senior counsel appearing
for the petitioner has provided us today with a compliance
table which identifies each and every stakeholder involved
in the implementation of the ‘Victim Protection Plan’. 
4. The stakeholders involved are as under:-
(i) All Authorities
(ii) State Governments and Departments
(iii) High Courts
(iv) Magistrates
(v) Anti Human Trafficking Units 
(vi) Rescue Teams and Leaders
(vii) NGOs and NGO Workers
(viii) Protective Homes
(ix) Social and Case Workers
(x) DLSA and Lawyers
(xi) Police Officers and Police Stations
(xii) Child Welfare Committees
(xiii) Medical and Mental Health Professionals
(xiv) Crime Records Bureau
(xv) Committees Overseeing Protective Homes
(xvi) Anti-Human Trafficking Cell
5. Thereafter, in the note, the learned senior counsel has
delineated the exact ‘Roles and Duties’ assigned to each
stakeholder under the ‘Victim Protection Plan’ in a tabular
format  and  also  indicated  the  corresponding
paragraphs/clauses from our judgment for ease of reference.
4

--- Page 211 ---
The  learned  senior  counsel  is  of  the  view  that  this
tabulation would better enable each stakeholder to grasp and
understand the nature and extent of responsibilities cast
upon them under the Victim Protection Plan.
6. The  learned  senior  counsel  has  undertaken  a  very
commendable exercise and it will go a long way in monitoring
the compliance of our directions. 
7. We also heard Ms. Aishwarya Bhati, the learned A.S.G,
appearing for the Union of India.
8. Ms. Aishwarya Bhati has provided us with a status note
highlighting what all has been done so far after the
judgment was pronounced by this Court. The note specifically
deals with the compliance of the additional directions
issued by us under paragraph 456 of the main judgment.
9. A plain reading of the status note furnished by the
learned A.S.G. reveals that the four additional directions
issued by us have not been fully complied with by all the
States/UTs, as on date. 
10. We would like to remind the all States/UTs that, (i)
notifying “recognized welfare institutions/organisations” in
accordance with the explanation to Section 15(6A) ITPA and
for the purpose of Section 17A ITPA, (ii) preparation of a
State/UT-wide list of social welfare workers eligible to
form a part of the non-official advisory board under Section
13(3)(b) ITPA and the panel maintained by the Magistrate
under Section 17(5) ITPA, (iii) designation of a Police
Nodal Officer (PNO), and (iv) designation of a Government
5

--- Page 212 ---
Nodal  Officer  (GNO),  are  absolutely  necessary  for  the
ground-level implementation of the ‘Victim Protection Plan’.
Therefore, by the next date of hearing, the Union of India
must ensure that the four additional directions as mentioned
in paragraph 456 of the main judgment are fully complied
with by all States/UTs.
11. The learned senior counsel appearing for the petitioner
has shared one copy of her compliance table today with the
learned A.S.G.
12. We are of the view that by the next date of hearing,
the Union shall call for the necessary information from all
the stakeholders referred to in the note furnished by the
learned  senior  counsel  appearing  for  the  petitioner,
inquiring, in what manner each of the directions have been
complied with and what has been done so far for meaningful
implementation of the plan which we have provided in the
judgment.
13. We take the compliance table provided to us by the
learned counsel appearing for the petitioner as well as the
status note provided to us by the learned A.S.G on behalf of
the Union of India on record.
14. At this stage, the learned senior counsel appearing for
the petitioner brought to our notice two additional aspects
that need some urgent attention. 
15. First, the learned senior counsel would submit that the
Anti-Human Trafficking Unit (ATHUs) should be given status
of a police station, in accordance with the directions
6

--- Page 213 ---
contained in Paragraph 362 b(iii) at page no.205 of the main
judgment dated 29.05.2026, at the earliest.
16. In this regard, we direct all the State/UT Governments
in their respective Home Departments to give effect to this
direction  at  the  earliest  by  issuing  an  appropriate
notification, in accordance with law.
17. The Union shall also take up this issue at the earliest
with all the States/UTs and see to it that appropriate
notifications are issued.
18. Secondly, the learned senior counsel would submit that
certain guidelines pertaining to the ‘threshold inquiry’
which is to be conducted by the Magistrate under Section 17
ITPA, are necessary. 
19. In the ‘Victim Protection Plan’, at the stage of
production of the rescued victim(s) who are adults (above
the age of 18 years) before the Magistrate under Section 17
ITPA,  we  have  incorporated  some  detailed  directions
pertaining to the conduction of a ‘threshold inquiry’ to
identify voluntary sex workers and the manner in which their
release/rehabilitation must be proceeded with. In other
words,  the  need  for  an  additional/parallel  judicial
determination to identify voluntary sex workers, by the
Magistrate, within the framework of Section 17 ITPA, was
emphasized by us. The rationale behind the need for such an
inquiry  is  provided  under  paragraphs  330-356  of  our
judgment.
20. This judicial determination takes into account various
7

--- Page 214 ---
aspects including the consent of the rescued victim and her
views on whether she wishes to be placed under long-term
safe  custody,  her  statement  about  the  voluntary/non-
voluntary nature of her work, the social worker’s assessment
of said voluntariness, whether the victim’s position is
influenced by any threats of coercion/undue influence/force,
and whether there are any safety concerns placing the victim
at real or immediate risk of danger/re-trafficking upon
release, amongst others. 
21. This threshold inquiry as regards the voluntary nature
of  the  work  of  the  rescued  victim  is  triggered
notwithstanding the opinion expressed by the rescued victim
that her work is voluntary in nature. In other words, the
magistrate  must,  under  all  circumstances,  conduct  this
threshold  inquiry  to  determine  the  further  appropriate
course of action for the protection, rehabilitation and re-
integration of the rescued victim who is an adult. 
22. The learned senior counsel appearing for the petitioner
is of the view that this process needs to be articulated
clearly and appropriate training must be imparted to the
Magistrates across the country to enable them to implement
our directions both in letter and spirit. The learned senior
counsel is also of the opinion that the creation of such
guidelines and imparting such training would ensure that the
determination process is uniform across the country. 
To that aim, we request the National Judicial Academy to
prepare a comprehensive protocol/guidelines to enable the
8

--- Page 215 ---
Magistrates to conduct this inquiry. The Petitioner may
provide assistance to the academy in the preparation of such
protocol.
23. There is one another important aspect that we wish to
address. Time and again, we have observed that, although
this Court painstakingly issues a slew of directions in the
form of guidelines or sets up a framework to ensure that the
fundamental rights of citizens are safeguarded and enforced
in reality, yet once these directions are committed to the
paper in the form of a judgment, the matter marks its abrupt
end. This Court, more often than not, has no means of
knowing whether the frameworks, guidelines or plans are
making any measurable differences in people’s lives, or what
hindrances stand in the way. The same anxiety grips us here.
We have put in place a thorough ‘Victim Protection Plan’ but
cannot tangibly ascertain whether it is having the desired
impact or faltering in its implementation. To help us gauge
this, we would like to hear from both the Petitioner and the
Union of India on how they and other involved stakeholders
can help us track progress and measure impact. 
24. By the next date of hearing, let a fresh status report
be placed on record by the Union of India. We would also
like to the petitioner to provide us a fair idea of the
progress made by the National Judicial Academy in connection
with the preparation of the aforesaid protocol/guidelines
for Magistrates. Lastly, we expect both the petitioner and
the Union to suggest concrete ways and methods that we can
9

--- Page 216 ---
adopt to track the real implementation, progress and impact
of the ‘Victim Protection Plan’. 
25. Post this matter on 14th December, 2026.
