          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Delay condoned.
2. These are petitions and cross petitions, challenging the
correctness  of  the  judgment/order  dated  19-08-2024  in  WA
No.330/2023  and  judgment/order  dated  15-12-2025  in  REP
No.238/2025 passed by a Division Bench of the Gauhati High
Court. By the said judgment/order(s), the High Court set aside
the judgment of the learned Single Judge dated 12.06.2023.
3. Heard  Mr. Narender Hooda, learned Senior Counsel for the
National Highways and Infrastructure Development Corp. Ltd.
(for short, ‘NHIDCL’)-petitioner(s)/respondent(s) and Mr.Amit
Anand Tiwari, learned Senior Counsel for the Girin Deka-
respondent(s)/petitioner(s) in these matters.
4. The respondent(s)- Girin Deka filed Writ Petition (Civil)
No.7326/2018 before the Gauhati High Court seeking writ of
mandamus  directing  release  of  a  contractual  amount  of
Rs.11,06,85,770/- by NHIDCL.
5. The learned Single Judge, on 12.06.2023, allowed the writ
petition and directed the release of payment while allowing

--- Page 219 ---
3
NHIDCL to pursue remedies to recover any amounts, if any due
from M/s.Corsan Corviam Construction S.A..
6. The matter was carried in appeal to the Division Bench of
the High Court by NHIDCL. The Division Bench, by the impugned
order(s), while holding that in a contractual dispute of the
nature that arose in this case, it was not appropriate to
invoke the writ jurisdiction since disputed question of facts
were involved, allowed the appeal with certain observations.
7. The observations of the Division Bench in paragraph
Nos.14, 20, 21 to 29 & 32 of the impugned order(s) dated
19.08.2024 were as under:
“14. It is trite that in a matter involving contractual
disputes, remedy in the form of a writ petition would
not be the appropriate remedy, more so, if there are
disputed question of facts involved in the matter.
Disputes  arising  within  the  realm  of  the  contract
agreement ought to be resolved by seeking remedy before
the forum designated by the contract agreement. In the
present case, clause 26.3.1 of the contract agreement
dated  19/11/2014  contains  an  Arbitration  agreement,
according to which, disputes and difference between the
parties to the contract is required to be resolved by
referring the disputes to Arbitral Tribunal. However,
the fact remains that the sub-contractor is not a
signatory  to  the  agreement  dated  19/11/2014  and
therefore, clause 26.3.1 would not be applicable to it.
XXXXX
XXXX
20. For the reasons stated above, we are of the opinion
that the impugned judgement and order dated 12/06/2023
is unsustainable in law and hence, liable to be set
-aside by this Court.”

--- Page 220 ---
4
“21. Having held as above, we are also conscious of the
fact that the sub-contractor M/s. Girin Deka, is a
proprietorship firm registered under the Micro, Small
and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006 (here-in-
after referred to as the Act of 2006). The Act of 2006
has been enacted by the Parliament for the purpose of
facilitating promotion, development and enhancing the
competitiveness of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises
and  for  matters  connected  therewith  or  incidental
thereto. From the object clause of the Act of 2006,8
apparent that the object of the Act of the 2006 is to
protect and promote the interest of Micro, Small and
Medium Enterprises.
22. Section 2(d) of the Act of 2006 defines 'buyer',
which reads as follows:-
“"Buyer" means whoever buys any goods or receives
any service from a supplier for consideration."
23. There is no dispute about the fact that the sub-
contractor comes within the definition of "supplier" as
provided in section 2(n) of the Act.
24. A careful analysis of the admitted facts of this
case, in our opinion, prima facie establishes a "Buyer-
Supplier"  relationship  between  the  appellant  no.  1
(NHIDCL)  and  the  sub-contractor  falling  within  the
scope and ambit of the Act of 2006.
25. Section 15 of the Act of 2006 reads as follows :-
"15. Liability of buyer to make payment.-
Where any supplier, supplies any goods or renders
any services to any buyer, the buyer shall make
payment therefor on or before the date agreed upon
between him and the supplier in writing or, where
there is no agreement in this behalf, before the
appointed day:
Provided that in no case the period agreed upon

--- Page 221 ---
5
between the supplier and the buyer in writing
shall exceed forty-five days from the day of
acceptance or the day of deemed acceptance."
26. Section 16 of the Act lays down the procedure for
recovery of interest and the dues payable to the Micro,
Small and Medium Enterprises, which reads as follows :-
16. Date from which and rate at which interest is
payable.-
Where any buyer fails to make payment of the amount
to the supplier, as required under section 15, the
buyer shall, notwithstanding anything contained in
any agreement between the buyer and the supplier or
in any law for the time being in force, be liable
to pay compound interest with monthly rests to the
supplier on that amount from the appointed day or,
as the case may be, from the date immediately
following the date agreed upon, at three times of
the bank rate notified by the Reserve Bank."
27. Section 17 of the Act of 2006 creates an obligation
on the buyer to pay the amount due to the supplier
along with the interest thereon. Section 17 reads as
follows :-
17. Recovery of amount due.-
For any goods supplied or services rendered by the
supplier, the buyer shall be liable to pay the
amount  with  interest  thereon  as  provided  under
section 16,"
28. Section 18 of the Act of 2006 lays down the
procedure to be followed for the purpose of making a
reference  to  Micro  Small  and  Medium  Enterprises
Facilitation Council. Section 18 is reproduced herein
below for ready reference :-
"18.  Reference  to  micro  and  small  enterprises
facilitation council.-
1. Notwithstanding anything contained in any other

--- Page 222 ---
6
law for the time being in force, any party to a
dispute may, with regard to any amount due under
section 17, make a reference to the Micro and Small
Enterprises Facilitation Council. 
2. On receipt of a reference under sub-section (1),
the Council shall either itself conduct mediation
itself or refer the matter to any medication service
provider as provided under the Medication Act, 2023.
3. The conduct of mediation under this section shall
be as per the provisions of the Mediation Act, 2023.
4. Where the mediation initiated under sub-section
(3) is not successful and stands terminated without
any settlement between the parties, the Council
shall  either  itself  take  up  the  dispute  for
arbitration or refer it to any Institution or centre
providing alternative dispute resolution services
for such arbitration and the provisions of the
Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (26 of 1996),
shall,  then  apply  to  the  dispute  as  if  the
arbitration  was  in  pursuance  of  an  arbitration
agreement referred to in sub-section (1) of section
7 of that Act.
5. Notwithstanding anything contained in any other
law for the time being in force, the Micro and Small
Enterprises  Facilitation  Council  or  the  centre
providing alternative dispute resolution services
shall have jurisdiction to act as an Arbitrator or
Mediator under this section in a dispute between the
supplier located within its jurisdiction and a buyer
located anywhere in India."
29. From a plain reading of the provisions of the Act of
2006, it is thus apparent that the Act of 2006 is a
Special Statue, enacted by the Parliament with the
objective of protecting the right of the Micro, small
and Medium Enterprises. The fact that section 18 of the

--- Page 223 ---
7
Act  of  2006  begins  with  a  non-obstante  clause  is
sufficient to indicate that the entitlement of the Micro
provided under the Act, would have an overriding effect
over any other law for the time Small and Medium
Enterprises  to  recover  its  lawful  dues  by  taking
recourse to the mechanism being in force. Therefore, in
the event, any MSM Enterprise, coming within the ambit
of the Act of 2006, is wrongfully denied payment for the
goods delivered or services rendered by it, than in that
event, regardless of any other law for the time being in
force to the contrary, the enterprise will be entitled
to recover its dues by taking recourse to section 18.
Section 18 of the Act of 2006, in our view, not only
provides an adequate and efficacious remedy to the MSM
Enterprise to recover its legitimates dues but the same
also  provides  an  opportunity  to  fast-track  the
resolution of all such disputes.
XXXXXX
32. This writ appeal is being disposed of by granting
liberty to the sub-contractor (respondent Nos 1 & 2
here-in) to invoke section 18 of the Act of 2006 for
recovery  of  its  Facilitation  Council,  having
jurisdiction over the dispute, for resolution of the
same in dues. The matter be, accordingly, referred to
the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises accordance with
the scheme of the Act of 2006.”
8. The net result was, after holding the writ petition to be
not  maintainable,  observations  were  made  about  the
maintainability of a claim before the Micro, Small and Medium
Enterprises Facilitation Council under the Micro, Small and
Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006 (for short, MSMED
Act’).
9. Mr. Narender Hooda, learned Senior Counsel for NHIDCL

--- Page 224 ---
8
submits  that  having  held  the  writ  petition  to  be  not
maintainable and having reversed the learned Single Judge
finding on that score, the Division Bench of the High court
ought not to have made the above observations.
10. Learned Senior Counsel for NHIDCL submits that if at all
the  respondent(s)-Girin  Deka  had  any  right  to  maintain
proceedings under the Facilitation Council of the MSMED Act or
any other body, it was upto them to do so and for those
authorities/body  to  decide  the  maintainability  of  those
proceedings and adjudicate the claim, if any, on merits.
11. On the other hand, Mr. Amit Anand Tiwari, learned Senior
Counsel  for  respondent(s)-Girin  Deka  submits  that  learned
Single Judge was right in issuing a mandamus for release of the
subject amount and that these were admitted dues.  Mr. Amit
Anand Tiwari, learned Senior Counsel deferred the observations
in the impugned order(s).
12. We have carefully considered the submissions made by the
learned Senior Counsel for the parties. We are of the opinion
that the Division Bench of the High Court was right in
reversing the order(s) of the learned Single Judge and holding
that writ was not maintainable on the facts of the case. We are
also of the opinion that having held the writ to be not
maintainable, the Division Bench of the High Court could not
proceeded with and made the observations that it made in
paragraph 21 to 29 thereof. We, therefore, set aside the
observations of the Division Bench in paragraph 21 and 29
thereof. We also set aside the observation in paragraph 32

--- Page 225 ---
9
where conclusive findings on the jurisdiction of Facilitation
Council under the MSMED Act has been recorded.
13. Having said that, we leave open the remedies that are
available in law, to the respondent(s)-Girin Deka. As and when
that remedies are resorted to before any Fora/Body/Authority,
the said Fora/Body/Authority will decide the maintainability of
the said proceedings and wherever necessary the merits of the
claim.
14. All contentions are left open between the parties.
15. For the reasons stated above, while upholding the finding
of the Division Bench of the High Court about the non-
maintainability of the writ filed by the respondent(s)-Girin
Deka, we set aside the portions referred to above. 
16. Mr. Amit Anand Tiwari, learned Senior Counsel for the
respondent(s) submits that already proceedings are pending
before the MSMED Facilitation Council pursuant to the impugned
order(s).
17. If that be so, they are at liberty to pursue the said
proceedings. However, we make it clear that the objections
including jurisdiction of MSMED would be open for NHIDCL.
18. Needless to observe that the Facilitation Council will
decide those objections uninfluenced by any of the observations
made in the impugned order(s) as well as in the present order.
19. Since,  the  dispute  pertains  to  2017-2018,  the
Facilitation Council shall dispose of the matter within a
period of six months from today.
20. Both the Special Leave Petitions are disposed of in the

--- Page 226 ---

above terms.
21. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed
of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
 
CIVIL APPEAL NO.                          OF 2026 
(Arising out of SLP (C) No.22769 of 2023) 
 
UHL Power Company Limited                      ...Appellant(s) 
 
 
Versus 
 
The State of Himachal Pradesh                     ...Respondent(s) 
 
O R D E R 
Leave granted. 
2. At the stage of execution, dispute arose as to how the 
interest component must be calculated as per the partial 
modification made by this Court to the order of the High Court 
under Section 37 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 19961; 
which interfered with the Arbitration Award . Whether 
compound interest is applicable or not, was the essential 
question raised. 
3. Heard Sri Jaideep Gupta,  learned Senior Counsel for 
the appellant and Sri Navin Pahwa, learned Senior Counsel for 
the respondent. 
4. Sri Jaideep Gupta, learned Senior Counsel for the 
appellant, specifically read the judgment of this Court , 
 
1 Hereinafter referred to as ‘the Act’ 

--- Page 238 ---
Page 2 of 8 
 
 
produced as Annexure P4, and vehemently submitted that the 
entire pre-claim interest capitalized annually has been given 
a go-by, which seriously prejudices the appellant herein. The 
claim of Rs.26,08,89,107.35/ - has been reduced to 
Rs.9,10,26,558.74/- by the High Court , which was interfered 
with by this Court. The challenge made from the execution 
ended in the impugned judgment, which directed the order of 
the High Court to be followed, which is grossly irregular.  
5. Sri Navin Pahwa, learned Senior Counsel for the 
respondent, however, submits that there can be no claim set 
up for interest on the pre-claim amounts and whatever interest 
has been granted for the period when the matter was pending 
in arbitration, was paid, @9% and after the date of Arbitration 
Award till payment ; @18%. There is no further c ause to be 
agitated, is the contention. 
6. To better understand, we must look at the reliefs 
granted at the various stages . In the Arbitration Award, in 
addition to an  amount of Rs. 26,08,89,107.35/- on account of 
expenses incurred, interest @9% from the date of filing the 
claim before the Arbitration Tribunal till the date of the Award 
i.e.12.05.2003, was granted. There were also amounts granted 
under the head of general damages and costs. The counter 

--- Page 239 ---
Page 3 of 8 
 
 
claim raised by the State was declined by the Arbitrator. In the 
appeal by the State against the Award and the rejection of the 
counter claim, the award was set aside and the counterclaim 
stood allowed under Section 34 of the Act. Under Section 37 of 
the Act, the Division Bench of the High Court found that there 
is no question of compound interest being payable and it was, 
hence, that the interest was awarded at only 6% for the 
expenses incurred. The amounts awarded under general 
damages and costs were deleted completely. The counter 
claim also was declined.  
7. Before this Court, considering the change in law, it was 
held that the grant of interest component as coming out from 
paragraph 54(a) of the order under Section 37 of the Act, shall 
stand modified and the interest granted by the Tribunal , 
restored. The question was as to whether the restoration was 
with respect to the interest of 9% and 18% respectively for the 
period when the arbitration was pending and after the Award 
was made, or did it reckon the capitalised interest for the pre-
claim period as allowed by the Arbitrator.  
8. To understand the question referred, we must look at 
the Award and the order passed under Section 37 of the Act , 
with respect to the specific quantum on which the dispute is 

--- Page 240 ---
Page 4 of 8 
 
 
raised. Insofar as the damages, the Arbitral Tribunal indicated 
three aspects as having been claimed by the appellant, which 
are as under: 
‘(i) Rs.26,08,89,107.35 as expenses as per  
Annexure-A 
(ii) Rs.20 crores as general damages and 
(iii) Rs.186.27 crores for loss of expected profits’ 
 
  In fact, Annexure A was a computation produced by the 
claimant, which has been accepted in toto without referring to 
how the quantum has been arrived at. In this context, we must 
briefly notice the facts which led to the arbitration.  
9. By an advertisement dated 29.10.1990, the State of 
Himachal Pradesh invited offers for the development of ten 
hydro-electric projects in the State  in consonance  with the  
policy guidelines issued by the Government of India.  A 
Memorandum of Understanding was signed with the appellant 
herein on 10.02.1992. The facts indicate that to examine the 
feasibility of a 70 MW Hydro Electric Plant on uhl, a tributary 
of the river Beas, surveys were conducted for 5  ½  years. On 
the project report of Hydro Electric Plant with capacity of 100 
MW, with an enhanced project value of over 40%, an 
implementation agreement was signed on 22.08.1997. The 
project met with rough weather and eventually a request for 
arbitration was made on 11.07.2000, which resulted in 

--- Page 241 ---
Page 5 of 8 
 
 
appointment of an Arbitrator under Section 11 of the Act by the 
High Court on 10.01.2003.  
10. To understand the quantum on expenses, we extract the 
following from paragraph 51  of the judgment of the High 
Court: 
‘51. xxx             xxx                       xxx 
A chart submitted by appellant before learned 
Tribunal to which our attention was drawn by 
learned counsel for the respondent / State gave a 
break-up of the claim with regard to expenses 
and interest. The chart reveals that the 
expenditure claimed from the  years 1991 -92 to 
2002-03 was ₹9,10,26,558.74 on which compound 
interest was claimed @ 14% per annum for the 
years 1991-92 to 1994-95, 15% per annum for the 
years 1995-96 and 1996 -97, 16% per annum for 
the years 1997 -98 and 1999 -2000 at 12% per 
annum for the years 2000-01 to 2002-03, Both the 
principal amounts and the rates of interest were 
accepted by learned Tribunal but in our 
considered view learned Arbitrator / Tribunal fell 
in error in awarding compound interest in the first 
instance and thereafter interest on interest both 
pendente lite and future till realization.’ 
 
11. From the above extract, it is seen that from 1991-92 to 
2002-03, interest has been granted for the expenses incurred 
in the total period between 1992 -2003. We are unable to 
countenance as to how the interest was granted at varying 
rates for different periods and for what reason it was 
capitalised. No reasoning comes forth from the Award. The 

--- Page 242 ---
Page 6 of 8 
 
 
quantum of expense was during the project and it cannot 
definitely commence from the very inception in the year 1992; 
which presumably led to the High Court to reduce the Award 
on account of expenses to Rs. 9,10,26,558.74/-, being the 
principal amount, with simple interest @6% per annum, from 
the date of filing of the claim till the date of realization of the 
awarded amount. The future interest was also consequently 
deleted. 
12. In the appeal before the Hon’ble Supreme Court, this 
Court found so in paragraph 6, which is extracted hereunder: 
‘6. As the judgment in the case of S.L. Arora(2010) 3 SCC 
690, on which reliance has been placed by the 
Division Bench of the High Court of Himachal 
Pradesh, has since been overruled by a three-Judge 
Bench of this Court in the case of Hyder Consulting 
(UK) Ltd.(2015) 2 SCC 189 , the findings returned by the 
Appellate Court in the impugned judgment to the 
effect that the Arbitral Tribunal is not empowered to 
grant compound interest or interest upon interest 
and only simple interest can be awarded in favour 
of UHL on the principal amount claimed, is quashed 
and set aside. As a result, the findings returned in 
para 54(a) of the impugned judgment insofar as it 
relates to grant of the interest component, are 
reversed while restoring the arbitral award on the 
above aspect in favour of UHL.’ 
(underlining by us for emphasis) 
 
13. The argument of  the learned Senior Counsel for the 
appellant is based on the portion of the order underlined as 
above, with reference to paragraph 2, wherein the appellants 

--- Page 243 ---
Page 7 of 8 
 
 
contention of an Award of a sum of Rs. 26,08,89,107.35/- was 
granted, being the pre -claim expenses with the interest 
capitalized annually, was recorded.  
14. The High Court interfered with the expenses computed 
and the capitalised interest reckoned for the pre -claim 
component to bring it down to the principal amount claimed. 
The High Court also reduced the interest component for the 
period when the arbitration was pending and by inference 
deleted the post award interest too. The modification made, in 
addition to deletion of the counter claim was in Paragraph 
54(a) of the judgment of the High Court under Section 37 of the 
Act as extracted below: 
(a) ₹9,10,26,558.74, is awarded as the actual 
principal amount along with simple 
interest at the rate of 6% per annum from 
the date of the filing of the claim till the 
date of the realization of the awarded 
amount; and’ 
 
 
15. Juxtaposed with the above extract, when we read the 
order of this Court, we can only come to a conclusion that the 
grant of interest alone was restored as per the Award , which 
would be @9% between the date of claim and the date of 
Award and later @18%. It goes without saying that the Award 
@9% and @18% would stand capitalized annually in the two 

--- Page 244 ---
Page 8 of 8 
 
 
periods i.e., the interest component of each year would be 
added to the principal  amount, for computing the further 
interest for the next year and so on.  In so far as the pre -claim 
period, we cannot understand this Court to have restored the 
capitalized interest. 
16. With the above observation, the impugned order is 
modified, and the execution shall be in accordance with our 
directions. 
17. The appeal is allowed. 
18. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand rejected.

                (J. B. PARDIWALA)

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
EXTRAORDINARY APPELLATE JURISDICTION
SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CIVIL) No.16092/2025
BOMBAREDDY ASHOK REDDY                          PETITIONER(s)
                                VERSUS
MS PANCHAJANYA FEATURES THROUGH ITS 
DIRECTOR MR SHRAVAN JESTA & ANR.     RESPONDENT(s)
O R D E R
1. The parties were referred for mediation to the Supreme
Court Mediation Centre.
2. We are informed by the learned counsel appearing for the
parties that the mediation has been successful. The Settlement
Agreement dated 25.04.2026 has been reduced into writing, duly
signed by the parties, their respective counsel, including the
learned Mediator.
3. The terms of the settlement reads thus:-
“WHEREAS
A. This Settlement Agreement is entered into between
Petitioner- Mr. Bommareddy Ashok Reddy S/o Chandra Shekar
Reddy, R/o 4303, 4th Block, Panchavati Apartments, Pragati
Nagar,  Kukatpalli,  Hyderabad-500090  (herein  after
referred  to  as  Petitioner)  and  Respondents  M/s
Panchajanya features Through Its Director Mr Shravan
Jesta and Others, having registered office at flat no. A-
702,  Honer  Vivantis,  Gopanpalli,  Serlimgampally,
Hyderbad-500046, Telangana (herein after referred to as
Respondent).
B. First Party is a script writer who filed a suit for
Permanent Injunction vide O.S No. 268/2024 against Second
Party for Copyright Infringement, before the Ld. District
Judge at L.B Nagar, Ranga Reddy District in Telangana,
along  with  an  additional  Interim  Application  No.
1

--- Page 255 ---
408/2024,  seeking  Ad-interim  Injunction  to  restrict
Second Party from releasing any related material to the
Film 'Vinnapalu Vinavale Vintha Vinthalu'.
C. Pursuant to the suit filed by the First Party, Second
Party, filed an Application before the Ld. District Judge
under  Order  VII  Rule  11  of  CPC,  challenging  the
jurisdiction of the Court on the ground that the dispute
between the parties is a commercial dispute directly
covered by the Commercial Courts and therefore, Civil
Court does not have jurisdiction to entertain the Suit.
However, the application filed by the Second Party was
dismissed by the Ld District Judge, vide its Order dated
15.07.2024.
D. Aggrieved by the Order dated 15.07.2024, the Second
Party approached the Hon'ble High Court of Telangana vide
Civil Revision Petition No. 2323 of 2024 filed under
Article 227 of the Constitution of India, whereby the
Hon'ble High Court while allowing the petition set aside
the order passed by the Ld. District Judge, vide its
Order dated 02.05.2025.
E. Order of the Hon'ble High Court was challenged by the
First Party before the Hon'ble Supreme Court in SLP
(Civil) No. 16092 of 2025, whereby the Hon'ble Supreme
Court was pleased to refer the parties for mediation,
vide its order dated 18.08.2025. The Parties appeared
before the Supreme Court Mediation center, however, could
not reach an amicable settlement.
F. When the case was listed for hearing on 02.12.2025,
the Hon'ble Court recorded that "We find no merit in the
matter and we could have dismissed it today itself.
However,  a  proposal  has  been  put  forward  by  the
petitioner before the respondent for settlement. 2. The
Parties to appear before the Supreme Court Mediation
Centre on 16.12.2025 and work out the terms of the
settlement. 3. It is understood that the respondent-
original defendant shall pay an amount of Rs.13,00,000/-
(Rs. Thirteen lakhs only) to the petitioner-original
plaintiff towards full and final settlement. 4. List
after  the  mediation  report  is  received." With  that
observation, the Parties were directed to appear before
the Supreme Court Mediation Centre to work out the terms
of settlement.
G. Pursuant thereto, the Parties appeared before the Ld.
Mediator on 16.12.2025 and worked out the following terms
of settlement.
Terms of Settlement
1. The Petitioner is the author of an original story
intended  for  an  audiovisual  project  and  has  also
contributed his portion of screenplay work and rendered
2

--- Page 256 ---
services while working at the Producer's office. The
parties have agreed to resolve all rights, claims, and
entitlements  by  way  of  a  one-time,  full  and  final
settlement. It is agreed that the story shall be credited
in the name of Ashok Bommareddy, the story development
shall be carried out by other names as determined by the
Producer, and the screenplay shall be credited as " Ashok
Bommareddy and other names".
2. In consideration of all services rendered and rights
assigned, the Producer agrees to pay the Writer a lump-
sum amount of 12,00,000/- (Rupees Twelve Lakhs Only).₹
The said amount is accepted by the Writer (Petitioner) as
a  one-  time,  full  and  final  settlement  towards
consideration for the story, the Writer's portion of
screenplay work, and salary/remuneration for the Writer's
portion of work performed at the Producer's office. The
Writer acknowledges that no further payment, royalty,
profit share, or consideration of any nature whatsoever
shall be payable now or in the future.
3. The Petitioner hereby unconditionally, irrevocably,
and absolutely assigns in favour of the Respondent all
rights, title, and interest in respect of the story,
screenplay,  and  all  allied  literary  and  creative
material, including drafts, concepts, characters, and
dialogues. The Respondent shall be the sole, exclusive,
and perpetual owner of all such rights in all aspects,
formats, media, languages, and territories, present and
future. The Petitioner further waives, to the extent
permitted by law, all moral rights under Section 57 of
the Copyright Act, 1957, and confirms that he shall have
no ownership or claim post this Agreement. The Petitioner
agrees  and  confirms  that  this  Settlement  Agreement
constitutes a complete buy-out of his contribution and
that upon receipt of the settlement amount, he shall not
initiate or pursue any civil, criminal, commercial, or
other proceedings against the Respondent in respect of
the subject matter herein.
4. The Writer agrees and confirms that this Agreement
constitutes a complete buy out of his contribution and
that upon execution of this Agreement and receipt of the
aforesaid  amount,  he  shall  not  retain  any  right,
interest, claim, lien, or entitlement of any nature
whatsoever in relation to the story, screenplay, or the
project. The Writer (Petitioner) further agrees that he
shall not raise any claim in future, whether monetary or
otherwise,  including  claims  for  royalty,  authorship,
moral  rights,  injunction,  damages,  or  profit
participation.
5. The Petitioner shall maintain strict confidentiality
in  respect  of  the  story,  screenplay,  project,  all
intellectual property embodied therein, and the terms of
this Agreement, and shall not disclose, communicate,
3

--- Page 257 ---
publish, or make available the same to any third party in
any manner whatsoever, except as required by law or by
order of a court of competent jurisdiction, and it is
expressly agreed that any breach or attempted breach of
this obligation shall constitute a material breach of
this Agreement, rendering the Writer fully liable for all
consequences thereof, including bearing the entire cost
of litigation, court fees, advocate fees, expenses, and
damages, and entitling the Producer to seek all remedies
available in law and equity, including injunctive relief,
specific performance, and monetary compensation, without
prejudice to any other rights of the Producer.
6.  The  Petitioner  acknowledges  that  the  story,
screenplay, and all related materials are intellectual
property  under  the  Copyright  Act,  1957  and  other
applicable laws, and hereby irrevocably assigns to the
Producer  all  rights,  title,  and  interest  therein,
including copyright and allied rights, in all forms,
formats, media, languages, and territories, present and
future;  the  Writer  further  waives,  to  the  extent
permitted by law, all moral rights under Section 57 of
the Copyright Act, 1957 and agrees that he shall have no
ownership  or  claim  post  this  Agreement,  and  shall
maintain  strict  confidentiality  of  the  project,
materials,  and  terms  of  this  Agreement,  any  breach
whereof  shall  entitle  the  Producer  to  all  remedies
available  in  law,  including  injunctive  relief  and
damages.
7. It is pertinent to mention that out of the total
settlement amount of 12,00,000/-, a sum of 4,00,000/-₹ ₹
(Rupees Four Lakhs Only) shall be paid by the Respondent
to  the  Petitioner  at  the  time  of  signing  of  this
Settlement  Agreement,  and  the  balance  amount  of
8,00,000/- (Rupees Eight Lakhs Only) shall be paid₹
within 60 (sixty) days from the date of first payment of
Rs. Four Lakhs (Rs 4.00,000/-). Upon receipt of the
aforesaid  amount,  the  Petitioner  acknowledges  full
satisfaction of all claims and confirms that no claim of
any nature survives.
8. This Agreement constitutes the entire understanding
between the parties and supersedes all prior discussions,
negotiations, or communications. No amendment shall be
valid unless made in writing and signed by both parties.
This Agreement shall be governed by the laws of India,
and  courts  at  Hyderabad  shall  have  exclusive
jurisdiction.
9. That the Petitioner and the Respondent have agreed
that none of them will initiate any other legal action or
complaint against each other in respect of the same
dispute in future.
10. That by signing this Agreement the parties hereto
4

--- Page 258 ---
solemnly state and affirm that they have no further
claims or demands against each other and all the disputes
and differences have been amicably settled by the parties

11. The parties undertake to abide by the terms and
conditions set out in the above-mentioned terms of this
Settlement Agreement, which have been arrived with free
will of the parties without any coercion, duress or
collusion and parties undertake not to raise any dispute

12.  That  the  parties  are  accordingly  signing  this

13. The contents of this Settlement Agreement have been
explained to all the parties through their respective
counsels and they have understood and understood the same

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The Election Committee of the Supreme Court Bar Association
(SCBA)  shall  file  a  status  report  regarding  compliance  with
paragraph  20  of  our  order  dated  29.05.2026,  pertaining  to
incorporation of reforms in the SCBA Rules. Such status report
shall be submitted, in consultation with the Executive Committee of
the SCBA.
2. We also invite the suggestions and opinions of the Executive
Committee of the SCBA, the Supreme Court Advocates on Record
Association, the Delhi High Court Bar Association, and all the
District Bar Associations in the NCT of Delhi, as to why the
elections of all the Bar Associations should not be held on one
date. We request the learned counsel/representatives of the various
6

--- Page 267 ---
Associations to be present on the next date of hearing.
3. List  the  case  on  05.11.2026.  The  above  compliance
affidavits/submissions shall be filed and circulated among the
parties at least 4 days before the next date of hearing.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL  NO.       OF 2026
(@ SLP(CRL.) No.9877/2026)
GAYYUR                                         APPELLANT(S)
                                VERSUS
     THE STATE OF U.P.                             RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The appellant herein was charged for the offences under
Sections 121, 121-A, 122 and 123 of the Indian Penal Code,
1860  (for  short,  'the  IPC,  1860')  in  Sessions  Trial
No.820/2000 arising out of FIR No.106/2000. 
3. The Trial Court, vide judgment dated 18.05.2007, was pleased
to acquit the appellant for the following reasons:-
47. The Ld. Counsel of the accused persons has
advanced arguments that Gayur has been stated to be
a witness in respect of preparation of passport and
it has been deposed that Gayur was a witness to the
effect of passport preparation. In this regard, no
deposition  has  been  made  on  behalf  of  the
prosecution. It is correct that Gayur has been
stated to be a witness in respect of preparation of
passport and such evidence has not been adduced by
the prosecution and whatever the recoveries have
been  stated  to  be  effect  of  Tamanchas  and
cartridges from Gayur. Said trial is not pending
before this Court, therefore, sufficient evidence
is not available against Gayur. 

--- Page 283 ---
2
49. It has been contended during cross examination
on behalf of the accused persons that the police
has falsely got implicated Ashfaq for wreaking
vengeance against Pradhan Pati Munna he does not
know Waris and Waris has not been arrested from his
house  and  this  argument  is  not  supported  by
evidence and the PWs have succeeded in proving that
Mohd. Waris was arrested from the residence of
Ashfaq and Ashfaq was also arrested at the same
time.  Mohd.  Waris  has  been  residing  at  his
residence under his assumed/concealed identity and
he  was  involved  in  anti-India  activities,
accumulation of weapons, waging war against India
and hatching conspiracy of waging war etc. and all
such activities were jointly and individually were
there by Mohd. Waris and Ashfag and Ashfaq has
given shelter to Mohd. Waris and Waris got hand
grenades recovered from the residence of Ashfaq and
pistols  and  cartridges  were  also  got
recovered  from  the  residence  of  Ashfaq  and
therefore  the  arguments  advanced  during  cross
examination are not such as may inspire confidence.
50. On the basis of the abovesaid discussion I have
come to the inference that accused persons Mohd.
Waris and Ashfaq @ Nanhe have been found accused of
the  offence  U/S  121,  121A,  122  and  123
I.P.C. Accused Gayur and Sardar Ali deserve to be
acquitted of the offence U/S 121, 121A, 122 & 123
IPC for want of sufficient evidence against them.
Accused persons Mohd. Waris and Ashfaq are found
accused of the offence under Section 13/14 of the
Foreigners Act and accused Ashfaq @ Nanhe has also
been found  accused of the offence U/S 25 of the

--- Page 284 ---
3
Arms Act and offence against him U/S 27 of the Arms
Act does not stand sustained, therefore, he is
acquitted of the charge U/S 27 of the Arms Act.
Accused Mohd. Waris deserves to be acquitted of the
charge U/S 3 of the Passport Act and Section 3 of
the  Explosive  Substance  Act  due  to  technical
infirmities.”
4. Aggrieved, an appeal was filed by the State before the High
Court in Government Appeal No.6077/2007. The High Court, vide
judgment dated 05.06.2019, was pleased to confirm the order of
acquittal of the Trial Court  qua the appellant, while also
observing that the issue for want of sanction cannot be
faulted with. It was noted that the Trial Court, as stated,
did, in fact, go into the merits of the case and found that no
ground had been made out, even for maintaining one of the
charges against the appellant. 
5. Thereafter, the respondent obtained a sanction on 31.07.2020.
On that basis, fresh proceedings were sought to be initiated
against the accused person(s), including the appellant. The
appellant  invoked  Section  482  of  the  Code  of  Criminal
Procedure, 1973 (for short, the CrP.C., 1973)  inter alia,
contending that it is a case of double jeopardy. The High
Court, vide impugned judgment dated 17.08.2022, was pleased to
dismiss it on the ground that the earlier trial was without
jurisdiction for want of sanction under Section 196 of the
CrPC, 1973 and, therefore, the same having been obtained
thereafter,  the  appellant  cannot  seek  to  interdict  the

--- Page 285 ---
4
proceedings.  Aggrieved by the same, the appellant is before
us.
6. We have heard the learned counsel appearing for the appellant
and the learned counsel appearing for the respondent-State. 
7. This is the second round of litigation, strangely, in a
criminal case, touching upon the same charges, despite the
earlier round having become conclusive, inter se parties. 
8. On  a  perusal  of  the  judgment  of  the  High  Court  dated
05.08.2019,  which  has  become  final,  we  note  that
notwithstanding the detailed consideration of the lack of
material to establish the foundational facts against the
appellant, the order of acquittal of the Trial Court was
confirmed and the same has attained finality. 
9. In our considered view, the impugned order of the High Court
cannot be sustained in the eye of law. It is not as if the
earlier proceedings of the Trial Court can be termed as void
ab initio. In fact, the Trial Court found that there was no
basis or material to come to the conclusion that the appellant
committed any crime. The finding was to the effect that there
was no evidence available against the appellant. That decision
was put into challenge by the respondent - State and has been
confirmed by the High Court, vide order dated 05.08.2019. A
mere observation by the High Court, while dismissing the
appeal against the State, will not give jurisdiction to the
respondent-State to start all over again. The presumption of
innocence in favour of the appellant gets rather strengthened

--- Page 286 ---
5
in view of the dismissal of the appeal against acquittal. At
the cost of repetition, the earlier decision of the Trial
Court, as confirmed by the High Court, has attained finality.
Hence, initiating fresh proceedings, on the same set of facts
and evidence, would certainly warrant interference, as it
violates Article 20(2) of the Constitution of India, 1950. 
10. To put it differently, the respondent - State having chosen to
charge the appellant and, thereafter, conducted the trial,
cannot contend to the contrary that the earlier decision is a
nullity. In other words, had the Trial Court rendered a
conviction against the appellant, the respondent before us
would not have raised such a plea. Allowing the trial to
continue against the appellant would amount to reviewing the
order of acquittal which has attained finality, not only on
the ground of want of sanction, but also on merits. 
11. Though, we find that the allegations are quite serious, they
per se, would not constitute an offence, unless supported by
adequate materials. The Trial Court, on the earlier occasion,
has  already  found  total  lack  of  evidence  against  the
appellant. 
12. In such view of the matter, we set aside the impugned judgment
passed by the High Court, and consequently, the criminal
proceedings in Case No. 3131/2021 arising out of FIR No. 106
of 2000, pending on the file of Judicial Magistrate, Shamli at
Kairana, stands quashed insofar as the appellant is concerned.
13. The appeal stands allowed, accordingly.

1. Pursuant to our order dated 19.08.2026, Mr. Gopal Sankaranarayanan,
learned Amicus Curiae, has placed on record:
a. A chart analysing reasons for pendency of execution proceedings
across various courts;
b. A chart tabulating the views of the High Courts on the constitution
of District Execution Cells; and
c. The  judgments  of  the  Ld. Single  Judge of  the  Delhi  High  Court
dated 05.12.2019, 05.08.2020, and 24.06.2021.
2. We note that 17 High Courts 1 have supported the constitution of District
Execution Cells, while 4 High Courts2 have expressed their opposition. In
3  other  High  Courts3,  the  proposal  remains  under  consideration.  A
response has not been received from the High Court of Rajasthan. 
3. Of the 17 High Courts in favour, 3 [Allahabad, Jharkhand and Tripura] are
at  an  advanced  stage,  with  the  composition  and  the  process  of
1 Allahabad, Andhra Pradesh, Bombay, Calcutta, Chhattisgarh, Delhi, Gauhati, Jammu and Kashmir, Jharkhand,
Karnataka, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, Meghalaya, Patna, Sikkim, Tripura and Uttarakhand.
2 Himachal Pradesh, Madras, Manipur, Punjab and Haryana.
3 Gujarat, Orissa and Telangana.
1

--- Page 290 ---
nomination to choose members clarified. They are requested to fill up
vacancies and commence functioning at the earliest. The High Courts of
Allahabad, Jharkhand and Tripura are requested to file a report on their
experience  of  the  functioning  of  such  cells,  and  their  impact  on
pendency numbers, within 3 months.
4. The remaining 14 High Courts in favour are requested to take steps at
the earliest to evolve a governing framework for the Cells, and proceed
to  operationalize  them, including  by  integrating  into  such  Cells  any
existing mechanism for supervision of execution proceedings. They are
requested to file a progress report within 2 months.
5. The  3 High  Courts  which  are presently considering  the  proposal  are
requested to share their views before the next date of hearing.
6. We also note that some High Courts have expressed concerns regarding
funding, infrastructure and appropriate administrative assistance to the
District Execution Cells. The Ministry of Law and Justice, Union of India is
directed to file an affidavit in this regard, setting out measures that may
be  taken  to  facilitate  the  functioning  of  these  Cells,  and  may  also
nominate a designated person as the Nodal Officer for this purpose.
7. We  would  also  request  the  High  Courts,  as  an  interim  measure  to
designate the Secretary, District Legal Services Authority as the Member
Secretary of the respective District Execution Cell, who is an officer in
the cadre of the Civil Judge (Senior Division).   
8. The  High  Courts  shall  also  ensure that  the  Executing  Courts  call  for
affidavits of assets to be made by a judgment debtor under Form No.16A
of Appendix C of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 as is required under
Order XXI Rule 41 (2).  The District Execution Cell, wherever formed 
2

--- Page 291 ---
         
shall monitor the affidavits filed and carry out the following functions:-

attachment of assets and execution, along with proposed timelines
for each step. This plan shall immediately be placed before the

ii. The executing court shall then direct attachment/execution after

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL  NO. 12896 OF 2024
THE KARNATAKA PUBLIC SERVICE 
COMMISSION      APPELLANT
VERSUS
MR. SHAMASHUDDIN M. 
SAVADATTI & ORS.         RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1. We have heard learned counsel appearing for the respective
parties.
2. The appeal is at the instance of the Karnataka Public Service
Commission1. KPSC is aggrieved by the judgment and order of the
High Court of Karnataka at Bengaluru dated 18 th December, 2015 2,
whereby a writ petition 3 of the first respondent was allowed. He had
questioned in the writ petition an order dated 19 th May, 2010 of the
Karnataka Administrative Tribunal4 dismissing his original application.
While reversing the order of the Tribunal, a direction was issued by
the  High  Court  to  the  State  of  Karnataka  to  appoint  the  first
respondent to the post of Assistant Engineer in the 2A/PH category.
3. The brief facts giving rise to the original application before the
Tribunal  are  these.  The  first  respondent  applied  for  the  post  of
1 KPSC
2 impugned order
3 Writ Petition No.41267/2010 (S-KAT)
4 Tribunal
1

--- Page 297 ---
Assistant  Engineer  (Civil)  under  the  physically  handicapped
category/2B. In all, 21 posts were reserved by the KPSC for persons
with disabilities out of 648 available posts. The first respondent had
obtained an aggregate of 67.76% marks (pursuant to an interview
and written test) and was ranked 15 th. However, the KPSC did not
recommend  the  first  respondent  for  appointment  on  the  post  of
Assistant Engineer (Civil) on the ground that he fell within the 2B/PH
category, and there was only one seat reserved in that category
which was given to one Ayaz Pasha, who had scored 70.11%. In the
final selection list published by the KPSC, the first respondent’s name
did not feature. KPSC claimed that while there was one post reserved
under the 2A/PH category, the first respondent did not fall under the
2A/PH category and could not have felt aggrieved by selection of a
non-disabled  candidate  (one  Manjunath)  for  the  said  post  in  the
absence  of  non-availability  of  disabled  candidates.  Aggrieved
thereby,  the  first  respondent  approached  the  Tribunal  for  relief;
however, his application was dismissed. The High Court quashed the
order  of  the  Tribunal  and  allowed  the  writ  petition  of  the  first
respondent with the following observations/directions :
“18.  In  the  present  case,  admittedly  the  procedure  as
contemplated under the provisions of Sections 33 and 36 of the
said  Act  stated  supra,  has  not  been  followed  by  the  1 st
respondent,  while  filling  up  of  21  posts  reserved  for  disabled
persons. It is also not in dispute that respondent No 3 does not
belong to 2A/PH category and his name was not found in the
marks list and he is entirely from a different category in as much
as he does not belong to any one of the categories of different
physically handicapped categories. Therefore, the very selection
made by the 1 st respondent appointing the 3 rd respondent for the
2

--- Page 298 ---
reserved post 2A/PH category, is contrary to law. Admittedly, he
belongs to 2A category, but he is a non-disabled person. He has
been wrongly selected under 2A/PH category by the KPSC. The
same is impermissible in view of the provisions of Sections 33 and
36 of the said Act.
***
29. In view of the aforesaid reasons, writ petition is allowed in
part. The impugned order passed by the KAT dated 19th May, 2010
made in Application No.5971/2008 is hereby quashed. So also the
final selection list dated 16.10.2008 in so far as Mr. Manjunath
selection  of  respondent  No.3  H.M.,  under  2A/PH  category  is
quashed.  We  declare  that  the  petitioner  is  entitled  to  be
appointed to the post of Assistant Engineer (Civil) under 2A/PH
category.
30. However, we make it clear that though the 3 rd respondent
belongs to 2A-General category, he has been wrongly selected
under 2A/PH category. Since he has been in service for more than
7 years, it is open for him to approach the competent authority by
making  appropriate  representation  for  alternative  remedy,  if
permissible in accordance with law.”
4. Despite service of notice, the first respondent has not appeared
before us. However, the promotions earned by the first respondent
over a period of time since his original application before the Tribunal
was  dismissed  have  been  noted  by  us  in  our  order  dated  23 rd
September, 2026.
5. Much water has flown under the bridge since the Tribunal was
approached by the first respondent. Having perused the impugned
order, more particularly paragraphs 18, 29 and 30 extracted supra,
we find that observations/directions were made/given considering the
special facts of the case. Since the High Court, more than a decade
back, required the State to appoint the first respondent in the 2A/PH
category in place of the third respondent (Manjunath) while, at the
same time, it sought to protect his interest too by giving him the
liberty  to  approach  the  competent  authority  for  protection  of  his
3

--- Page 299 ---
service,  and  the  said  third  respondent  (Manjunath)  has  not
independently  preferred  any  appeal  challenging  quashing  of  his
appointment, it would not be prudent at this distance of time  to
disturb the findings which are based on the facts of the case. 
6. We, therefore, dispose of this appeal with the observation that
the  impugned  order  of  the  High  Court  shall  not  be  read  as  a
precedent  for  deciding  future  cases.  Whatever  benefit  the  first
respondent is entitled to, in terms of the impugned order, shall be
released to him, if not already released.
7. We also make it clear that if the State has not considered the
claim of the third respondent (Manjunath), it may do so now provided
he had made an approach in terms of the impugned order.

(DIPANKAR DATTA)

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
 
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.                          OF 2026 
(Arising out of SLP (Crl) No.16356 of 2026) 
 
Ajay Rameshwar Agrawal                      
  ...Appellant(s) 
 
Versus 
 
The Superintendent of Police CBI & Ors.   
...Respondent(s) 
 
O R D E R 
 
Leave granted. 
2. FIR-RC:8/E/2002/CBI/EOW/Mumbai was registered on 
29.10.2002 by the Economic Offences Wing (EOW) of the Central 
Bureau of Investigation (CBI) against the Officials of the IDBI Bank; 
arrayed as public servants and three private individuals, under 
various Sections of the Indian Penal Code , 1860  (IPC) and the 
provisions of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 1, also 
alleging criminal conspiracy. The allegation was that in collusion 
with the Officials of the Bank, the private individuals availed loans 
in the name of their companies , on the strength of fake invoices 
and delivery challans, indicating purported supply of equipment 
by fictitious companies and diverted the amounts disbursed by 
 
1 Hereinafter referred to as ‘the PC Act’ 

--- Page 303 ---
Page 2 of 6 
 
 
the Bank for other purposes. Allegation against the Officials of the 
Bank was with respect to the relaxation of terms and conditions for 
sanction and disbursement of loans to obtain illegal enrichment , 
bringing the case squarely under the PC Act.  
3. After conducting the investigation, the CBI decided to drop 
the charges against the Bank Officials and proceeded to file a 
chargesheet before the Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, 
19th Court, Esplanade, Mumbai as C.C. No.735/PW/2009. The 
appellant filed a discharge application under Section 239 of Code 
of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (CrPC), which was rejected. A  
revision was taken against the same  before the Sessions Court, 
Bombay unsuccessfully.   
4. The case was made over to the Additional CJM, 3rd Court, 
Esplanade, Mumbai, which proceeded to frame the charges 
rejecting the contention of the accused that the final report should 
have been filed before the Special Court. The ACJM found that the 
discharge prayed at the earlier instance was rejected and the 
contention of the Special Court alone having jurisdiction, was not 
urged in that earlier round. The contention of lack of jurisdiction 
was rejected by the Additional CJM’s Court and the High Court by 
the impugned order,  on the finding that the offences now 

--- Page 304 ---
Page 3 of 6 
 
 
charged, were only under the IPC and the Magistrate is 
competent to take cognizance and hold trial.  
5. The contention raised by the appellant is that , in fact, the 
police cannot decide as to the aspect of cognizance and their role 
is only to file a report, either finding material to frame charges or 
a closure report before the Competent Court and it would be up 
to the Court to decide as to whether there should be a cognizance 
taken. The appellant also relies on Sampat Singh and Others v. 
State of Haryana and Others2.  
6. Therein a complaint was made by an individual against a 
person holding a Cabinet rank in the Central Government, which 
was later withdrawn, allegedly on the complainant being offered 
a Chairman’s post in one of the  State Boards. Though, this Court 
in the cited decision refused to consider the plea made by the 
petitioners therein, but all the same  looked into the order of the 
Magistrate discharging the accused on the application for 
withdrawal made by the complainant. It was specifically noticed 
that in the said case registered under Sections 161 and 165 of the 
IPC and under Section 5 (2) of the PC Act, it could have been tried 
 
2 (1993) 1 SCC 561 
 

--- Page 305 ---
Page 4 of 6 
 
 
only by a Special Court. It was held that, in that circumstance, the 
Magistrate before whom the withdrawal report had been placed, 
ought to have forwarded the same before the Special Court, 
especially when the Magistrate had no power to try the offences. 
7. A slightly different situation arises in the present  case 
where the Investigating Agency has found that there is no case 
made out against the IDBI Officials and the only offences  that 
could be charged come under the IPC. The offences are also 
triable by a Magistrate and hence , the  chargesheet before the 
Magistrate.  
8. We immediately look at Section 157 CrPC which speaks of 
the ‘Procedure for Investigation’. On information received or 
otherwise, if an Officer-in-Charge of a police station has reason to 
suspect the commission of an offence , which he is  empowered 
under Section 156 to investigate, he is required to send a report  
of the same to the Magistrate, empowered to take cognizance of 
such offence upon a police report , forthwith and then by himself 
or deputing one of his subordinates, commence the investigation. 
9. In the present case , quite understanding the exclusive 
jurisdiction conferred on the Special Court, the FIR , on 
registration, was forwarded to the Special Judge, CBI, Mumbai, as 

--- Page 306 ---
Page 5 of 6 
 
 
is evident from Annexure P1 , along with the copies submitted to 
the Joint Director, DIG and DSP of the EOW of the CBI at Mumbai.  
10. It is trite that the final report filed before the Magistrate or 
the opinion of the Investigating Agency would not regulate the 
cognizance to be taken by the Court. The Court having 
jurisdiction to take cognizance would look into the report and 
either accept it or order further investigation or refuse to take 
cognizance; despite the Investigating Agency finding 
substantiation of the allegations or take cognizance ; even if the 
Investigating Agency ha s filed a closure report. Hence, the 
cognizance is within the exclusive domain of the Court having 
jurisdiction and it is only proper that the chargesheet be placed 
before the Special Judge, CBI, who will decide as to whether 
cognizance has to be  taken, even as against the IDBI  Officials. If 
the Special Judge accepts the report exonerating the IDBI 
Officials, then it is for the Special Judge to make over the case  to 
a Magistrate having jurisdiction, so as to enable cognizance of the 
offences under the IPC ; which then would be considered by the 
jurisdictional Magistrate.   
11. Hence, without any observation on the merits, we direct the 
Additional CJM, 3 rd Court, Esplanade, Mumbai, to 

--- Page 307 ---
Page 6 of 6 
 
 
forward/transmit the chargesheet filed to the Special Judge, CBI, 
Mumbai. 
12. We make it clear that we have not made any observations 
on the actual cognizance to be taken, which is a judicial act to be 
done by the Special Judge. 
13. The appeal is allowed with the above directions and  only 
to facilitate the transmission of the case to the Court having 
jurisdiction, we set aside the cognizance taken by the Additional 
CJM, on the technical ground as stated above, leaving the issue of 
cognizance to be considered by the Special Judge, CBI  or if h e 
accepts the report, to be considered by the jurisdictional 
Magistrate.  
14. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand rejected.

custom milling during the crop year 2023-2024, following
certain discrepancies, physical inspection was carried out
by  the  departmental  committees  which  estimated  a
shortage of 18,781 gunny bags of paddy this shortage was
equivalent  to  7,042.875 quintal  rice  causing  an  alleged
financial loss of Rs.2,04,25,573/- to the Government as well
as  Corporation  and  as  such  on  the  allegations  of

registered  by  the  husband  of  the  appellant  against  the
General Manager of the Corporation for alleged demand of
bribe.  Hence,  bail  applications  seeking  anticipatory  bail
filed in FIR No. 83/2025 came to be dismissed by the trial
Court and also by the High Court respectively. Hence, this
appeal.
4. It is the contention of the learned counsel appearing

the appellant and her husband is a retaliatory FIR in view of
the FIR No.12/2025 registered by the appellant’s husband

Criminal Appeal  No.4909/2026      Page   2   out of 4

--- Page 334 ---
5. Per contra, learned counsel for the respondent-State

the jurisdictional High Court. Even otherwise the appellant
being a lady also claims to be a partner who is not actively

This is an issue which will have to be thrashed out during
the course of the trial and as such we deem it proper to
make absolute the interim protection which was granted in

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION
ARBITRATION PETITION NO. 65 OF 2026
M/S. HANGZHOU QIANG TANG 
RIVEN ELECTRIC GROUP CO LTD PETITIONER(S)
VERSUS
MADHUCON PROJECTS LIMITED & 
ANR. RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. This petition has been filed under section 11(6) of the
Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (1996 Act) seeking
appointment  of  a  nominee  Arbitrator  on  behalf  of  the
Respondents for the adjudication of disputes that have arisen
between the parties.
2. The Petitioner is a company incorporated under the laws of the
People’s Republic of China and is engaged in the manufacture of
‘power and distribution transformers’. Respondent No. 1 is an
Indian company, based in Khammam, Andhra Pradesh, involved in
the infrastructure and construction business. Respondent No. 2
is also an Indian company, providing services, resources, and
assistance for setting up thermal power plants. 
3. Two Tripartite Agreements dated 13.02.2009 and 16.07.2010 (the
Subject Agreements) were executed between the Petitioner (as
1

--- Page 351 ---
manufacturer), Respondent No. 1 (as buyer), and Respondent No.
2 (as supplier) for the purchase of transformers, allied
equipment, and ancillary services for a coal-fired thermal
power plant of M/s Simhapuri Energy Private Limited. Under
Article 17.2 of the Subject Agreements, the disputes arising
out  of  the  Subject  Agreements  would  be  finally  settled
exclusively by arbitration. The arbitral tribunal is to consist
of three arbitrators, with the seat of arbitration being in
Hyderabad, India.
4. It  is  the  Petitioner’s  case  that  despite  performing  its
obligations  under  the  Subject  Agreements,  the  Respondents
failed to pay the bills raised by the Petitioner in terms of
the  billing  schedule,  leaving  a  sum  of  USD  629,874.10
outstanding.
5. The Petitioner initially issued a legal notice dated 08.05.2023
calling upon the Respondents to clear the outstanding amounts.
However,  due  to  non-compliance  by  the  Respondents,  the
Petitioner invoked the arbitration clause through notice dated
16.07.2023.  The  Petitioner  appointed  Mr.  Alladi  Ravinder,
Senior Advocate, as its nominee arbitrator and called upon the
Respondents  to  nominate  their  nominee  arbitrator.  The
2

--- Page 352 ---
Respondents have statedly not replied to the said notice,
leading to the Petitioner filing the instant Petition.
6. We have heard learned Counsel for the parties and perused the
material placed on record.
7. In view of the facts and circumstances recorded above, we deem
it just and proper to allow the instant petition and appoint
Justice R. Raghunandan Rao, former Judge of the Andhra Pradesh
High  Court,  as  the  nominee  arbitrator  on  behalf  of  the
Respondents. In the interest of expediency, we also appoint
Justice Matam Venkata Ramana, former Judge of the Andhra
Pradesh High Court, as the presiding arbitrator. The arbitral
tribunal of three learned arbitrators shall, thus, adjudicate
the disputes between the parties arising out of the Subject
Agreements.  The  seat  and  venue  of  the  arbitration,  in
accordance  with  the  said  Subject  Agreements,  shall  be
Hyderabad, India.
8. It  is  clarified  that  the  Arbitral  Tribunal  shall,  as  a
preliminary  issue,  examine  the  scope  of  the  arbitration,
including whether the Petitioner is entitled to invoke the
arbitration clause and whether the Petitioner falls within the
3

--- Page 353 ---
definition of “parties” for the purposes of reference of a
dispute to the Arbitrator.
9. All rights and contentions of the parties, including their
respective claims, counterclaims, and defences, as well as the
objections of Respondent No.1 as to the existence and scope of
the arbitration agreement, the effect of Article 17.4, and
limitation, are left open for determination by the learned
Arbitral Tribunal. The observations made hereinabove are prima
facie and shall not influence the Arbitral Tribunal in its
adjudication.
10. The Arbitral Tribunal shall be at liberty to fix its fee.
11. Pending application(s), if any, stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL No.4482/2016
THE STATE OF UTTAR PRADESH 
STATE OF UTTAR PRADESH 
THROUGH PRINCIPAL SECRETARY & ANR.            APPELLANTS
VERSUS
RAKESH KUMAR GUPTA                     RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1. We have heard Mr. S. R. Singh, learned senior counsel for the
appellants  in  support  of  the  appeal.  Learned  counsel  for  the
respondent is not called upon to answer.
2. The  Departmental  Promotion  Committee1 recommended  the
respondent  for  promotion  to  the  post  of  Additional  Municipal
Commissioner on 04th December, 2013. Such recommendation of the
DPC, however, became the subject matter of challenge in a writ
petition2 before the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad 3. On 11 th
December, 2013, the High Court stayed such recommendation. 
3. During the pendency of the aforesaid writ petition before the
High Court, a charge-sheet dated 07 th October, 2014 was issued to
the respondent in respect of alleged acts of commission/omission
amounting  to  misconduct.  The  incidents  in  respect  whereof  the
1 DPC
2 Service Bench No.-1736 of 2013 (Arun Rai & anr. v. State of U.P . & anr.)
3 High Court

--- Page 363 ---
2
charges had been levelled were of January, 2014 and July, 2014. 
4.  The inquiry, which had proceeded on the basis of the charge-
sheet dated 07th October, 2014, resulted in submission of a report of
the Inquiry Officer finding charge no.1 ‘partially proved’ and charges
2 and 3 ‘not proved’.
5. A  second  show  cause  notice  came  to  be  issued  to  the
respondent on 27th April, 2015, to which he duly responded.
6. In pursuance of partial proof of guilt recorded in respect of
charge  1,  the  respondent  was  punished  with  stoppage  of  two
increments on 18th December, 2025.
7. Meanwhile, on 23 rd February, 2015, the writ petition wherein
the  recommendation  of  the  DPC  was  questioned  came  to  be
dismissed  as  withdrawn.  Respondent,  thus,  urged  that  the
recommendation of the DPC be given effect.
8. Appellants,  in  view  of  the  outcome  of  the  disciplinary
proceedings, refused to act in terms of the recommendation of the
DPC and declined promotion to the respondent. 
9. Respondent  then  approached  the  writ  court  seeking
implementation of the DPC recommendation.
10. The High Court, vide a judgment and order dated 8 th January,
20164, allowed the writ petition of the respondent recording,  inter
alia, as follows:
“In the present case, accepted position is that on the date
when Departmental Promotion Committee has met, there
was no charge-sheet served upon the petitioner rather on
the strength of the interim order passed, his promotion
has been kept on hold and when the interim order has
been got vacated, the charge-sheet has been served and
4 impugned order

--- Page 364 ---
3
on the strength of the charge-sheet promotion order has
been kept on hold. Such keeping of promotion on hold is
not subscribed by law. In view of this, in the facts of the
case, the promotion in question cannot be kept on hold
and as such, respondents are directed to declare the result
of Departmental Promotion Committee and simultaneously
to conclude the disciplinary proceedings initiated against
the  petitioner  vide  charge-sheet  dated  07.10.2014  and
both the proceedings be completed within the same time
frame.”
11. The finding returned by the High Court is not disputed before
us. However, Mr. Singh seeks to rely on a notification dated 28th May,
19975. Relevant part of the said notification reads as follows:
“11. If  recommendation  has  been  made  for
promotion of any personnel by the Selection Committee,
but  before  implementation  of  order  of  promotion,
something as contained in Paragraph-2 comes out in the
knowledge, and had the same been before the Selection
Committee at the time of selection, then it would have
been  necessary  to  keep  the  recommendation  of  the
Selection Committee in a sealed cover, the concerned
personnel shall not be promoted and on receipt of the
final result of such proceedings, the recommendation of
the Selection Committee in respect of such personnel will
be implemented in such a manner under the provisions
of  this  Notification,  as  if  the  recommendation  of  the
Selection  Committee  was  kept  in  a  sealed  cover  in
respect of such personnel.”
12. According  to  him,  the  appellants  being  bound  by  such
notification could not have acted contrary to its terms; refusal to act
on the recommendation of the DPC was, therefore, just and proper. 
13. It is not in dispute that on the date the DPC assembled to
consider  the  case  of  the  respondent  for  promotion,  i.e.,  on  04th
December, 2013, no disciplinary proceeding was pending against the
respondent. Even the incidents giving rise to the charge-sheet dated
07th October, 2014 were not in existence. Having regard thereto, the
said  notification  would  have  no  application  on  the  facts  of  the
present case.
5 said notification

--- Page 365 ---
4
14. Even otherwise, we are of the considered opinion that the said
notification seeks to travel beyond the principles laid down in the
decision of this Court in Union of India v. K. V. Jankiraman 6 and,
in  a  way,  borders  on  overruling  the  same.  Although  legislative
overruling of judicial decisions is not unknown in law, the same is
permissible only in exceptional cases. This is not a case where the
said notification sought to remove the basis on which the principles
laid down in K. V. Jankiraman (supra) regarding adoption of ‘sealed
cover procedure’ were premised. Thus, the said notification cannot
be read in a manner so as turn such principles on its head.
15.   The High Court, in our further considered opinion, was perfectly
justified  in  allowing  the  writ  petition  of  the  respondent  by  the
impugned order.
16. There is absolutely no merit in this civil appeal, which stands
dismissed.
17. Now comes the question of relief. We have noted that while
granting leave on 25 th April, 2016, a coordinate Bench had stayed
the  operation  of  the  impugned  order.  In  view  thereof,  the
recommendation of the DPC could not be implemented.   
18. Since  the  respondent  has  retired  from  service  on  30 th
September, 2016 during the pendency of this appeal, he shall be
given promotion to the post of Additional Municipal Commissioner
with retrospective effect from the date his promotion fell due. He
shall be accorded all benefits, including financial benefits and arrears
of salary, as if he had been promoted when his turn arrived and also
6 (1991) 4 SCC 109

--- Page 366 ---
5
demitted  office  on  retirement  while  holding  the  said  post.  This
direction is made because the respondent cannot be held to be at
fault. His retiral benefits shall be calculated on the basis of the last
pay that he would have drawn on such promoted post. All benefits
be accorded to the respondent in accordance with law within 12
(twelve) weeks from date of production of a certified copy of this
order.
19. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.

  IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
    CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL No.________ OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP(Criminal) No.16283/2026)
CHHEDI SHARMA                                    Appellant(s)
                            VERSUS
THE STATE OF BIHAR                               Respondent(s)
     O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The  appellant  stands
convicted  by  the  Trial  Court  for
committing  offence  punishable  under
Section 307 of the Indian Penal Code,
1860  and  was  sentenced  to  undergo
rigorous imprisonment for 05 years by the
Trial  Court  vide  its  judgment  dated
05.12.2025 and order on sentence dated
12.12.2025.
3. During the pendency of the
appellant’s appeal before the High Court,
the appellant had prayed  for suspension
of sentence and his release on bail,

--- Page 381 ---
2
which has been rejected by the High Court
under the impugned order.
4. We  have  seen  the  findings
recorded by the Trial Court particularly,
under  paragraph  no.8  thereof  wherein,
while discussing the evidence of PW7, Dr.
Akhilesh Kumar, who examined the injured
PW8, Parmeshwari Sharma, has opined that
the injury sustained by PW8 over his head
was simple in nature though, caused by a
sharp cutting substance.
5. The appeal preferred by the
appellant before the High Court is of the
year  2026,  therefore,  there  is  least
likelihood of the appeal being heard in
the  near  future.  Moreover,  the
appellant’s  side  has  also  lodged  a
criminal case against the complainant and
thus, there are cross cases relating to
the  same  incident.  The  appellant  had
already  undergone  about  one  year  of
incarceration.
6. Thus,  considering  all  the
above broad features of the case, we are

--- Page 382 ---
3
of the considered view that the High
Court should have allowed the appellant’s
prayer for suspension of sentence.
7. Therefore,  we  are  of  the
considered view that it is a fit case to
suspend the sentence imposed upon the
appellant and enlarge him on bail.
8. Accordingly,  the  impugned

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL No.   OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) No.16436/2026)
PAVANKUMAR DHARMA CHAVAN ..... APPELLANT(S)
            
               VERSUS
THE STATE OF MAHARASHTRA ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. Appellant is aggrieved by order dated 19.06.2026,
passed by the High Court of Judicature at Bombay, Bench
at Aurangabad, (briefly the ‘High Court’ hereinafter),
rejecting  the  regular  bail  application  of  the
appellant.
4. Appellant has been named as an accused in Crime
Number 369 of 2024, registered with the Mukhed Police
1

--- Page 387 ---
Station  in  the  district  of  Nanded,  (State  of
Maharashtra), under Sections 318(4), 316(2), 336(2),
337, 338, 336(3), 340(2), 341(2), 296, 351(4), 238B and
61(2)(A), of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, (BNS).
5. Allegation against the appellant is that he was the
person behind organizing a racket to defraud unemployed
youths aspiring to secure Government employment. It is
alleged that approximately 1.1 crores were collected by
the co-accused on behalf of the appellant from various
aspirants seeking employment.
6. Appellant was arrested on 12.12.2024 and has been in
custody since then.
7. This Court by order dated 08.09.2026 had issued
notice,  pursuant  to  which  respondent  State  of
Maharashtra has filed counter affidavit.
8. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that out
of nine accused, eight have been enlarged on bail by
the Trial Court as well as by the High Court; only the
appellant  remains  behind  bars.  He  submits  that
investigation is complete and considering the period of
detention undergone by the appellant, further detention
would be unwarranted.
2

--- Page 388 ---
9. Per contra learned State counsel has referred to the
averments made in the counter affidavit and submits
that there is a difference between the appellant and
the other co-accused, appellant being the principal
mastermind of the entire operation. He further submits
that appellant has two criminal antecedents, one under
the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 of the year
2020, and the other pertaining to cheating, etc., of
the year 2021.
10. On a query by the Court as to whether the amount
allegedly defrauded from the job aspirants by the
accused  persons  has  been  recovered,  learned  State
counsel  submits  that  he  would  have  to  obtain
instructions. However, he submits that trial has been
delayed because of the discharge application being
filed by a co-accused for discharge.
11. Submissions made by learned counsel for the parties
have received due consideration of the Court.
12. Having  regard  to  the  fact  that  appellant  has
already undergone more than one year ten months of
incarceration, with investigation complete, we are of
the  considered  opinion  that  continuance  of  the
detention of the appellant is unwarranted.
3

--- Page 389 ---
13. Consequently, we set aside the impugned order of
the High Court dated 19.06.2026 and direct that the
appellant shall be produced before the Trial Court
within a maximum period of seven days from today,
whereafter he shall be enlarged on bail on such terms
and conditions as may be deemed appropriate.
14.  However, we direct that appellant shall cooperate
with the trial and not seek unnecessary adjournments.
15. Appeal is allowed.

16. Pending application, if any, shall stand disposed
of.

pending  before  the  jurisdictional  trial  court.  On  account  of  the  close

3

--- Page 395 ---
3. The  parties  have  appeared  before  this  Court.  On  previous
occasions, they have agreed that said settlement is voluntary, without
any force, threat or coercion and as such this Court finds no impediment
to accept the same and in fact, the parties had appeared physically /
virtually and they were identified by their respective learned counsels
and  in  token  of  having  identified  them,  learned  counsels   have  also
affixed their signatures.
4. The  earlier  agreement,  which  was  signed  before  the  learned
Mediator, is the one which has been referred to hereinsupra. However, on
account of the petitioner – wife having expressed certain reservations
with regard to the terms of the settlement, this Court was perforced to
refer the matter back to the mediator and despite all efforts, there was no
positive results which emerged from the subsequent mediation. Again the
parties appeared before this Court and subsequently the respondent –
husband offered additional sum of Rs.15,00,000/- to the two daughters,
namely, Rs.7,50,000/- payable after five years from 13.10.2026 to the
first daughter and Rs.7,50,000/- payable to the second daughter after ten
years from 13.10.2026. This additional condition which is accepted by
wife  has  now  been  incorporated  in  the  application  being  IA
No.322059/2026 filed on 13.10.2026 at paragraph No.14. In fact, this
clause should have been part and parcel of the agreement by way of a
supplemental agreement. For this lapse, the parties cannot be penalized.
Hence, we take lenient view in this regard and accept the same to avoid
further multiplication of litigation and hold that paragraph No.14 of the
4

--- Page 396 ---
application IA No.322059/2026 filed on 13.10.2026 shall be read as part
and parcel of the terms of the agreement dated 06.02.2026 which the
parties  have  agreed  to  before  this  Court  as  being  voluntary  when
specifically asked. In view of the same, the settlement agreement stands
accepted and despite the efforts for a reunion, same did not yield any
fruitful result and on account of the parties having agreed to part their
ways, the divorce as sought for is granted in exercise of the power under
Article 142 of the Constitution of India. Accordingly, the petitions stand
disposed of in terms of the settlement and the Registry is directed to
draw the decree in terms of the settlement agreement by incorporating
paragraph No.14 of IA No.322059/2026 filed on 13.10.2026 as part of the
decree which is also allowed. Since, it is agreed between the parties that
the pending proceedings can be closed, the matters / cases referred to in
paragraph No.3 of the settlement agreement stand disposed of / quashed
/ closed. 
5. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

to the Trust for the purpose of running this School in consonance
with Para 11 of our order dated 05.03.2025.

Inspection Report now on record. The Inspection Report, duly signed
by the Principal, Government Higher Secondary School, Ruabandha,
Bhilai and Principal, Government Higher Secondary School, Supela,
Bhilai-Durg, Chhattisgarh reads thus:-
“INSPECTION REPORT
 The college is a Post-Graduate College and not a school.
It was established in the year 1979.

courses. Enclosure 1

college is 1174 students, against the approved admission
capacity of 2,700 students. Enclosure 2a & 2b

Rs.49,795640)  Budget  and  Current  Year  Fee  Structure

Enclosure 4a and 4b

gracious enough to submit before this Court that they are ready and

CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION

SANDIP GHOSH              ...APPELLANT
