CENTRAL BUREAU OF INVESTIGATION  ...RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1) Leave granted.
2) The  appellant  has  been  chargesheeted  as  an
accused in connection with Special Case No.1 of
2025 arising out of CBI Case No.RC0102024A0007
dated 24.08.2024, registered at Central Bureau of
Investigation, Anti-Corruption Branch, Kolkata for
the offences punishable under Section 120-B read
with Sections 409, 420, 468 and 471 of the Indian
Penal  Code,  1860  (for  short,  ‘the  IPC’)  and
Sections  7,  13(2)  read  with  13(1)(a)  of  the
Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 (for short, ‘the
PC Act).  Aggrieved by the rejection of the bail
applications by the Special CBI Court  vide  order
dated 07.01.2025 as well as by the High Court vide
impugned order dated 23.02.2026 in CRM(M) No.1228
of 2025, the appellant is before us. 
3) We  have  heard  the  learned  senior  counsel
1

--- Page 415 ---
appearing  for  the  appellant  and  the  learned
Additional  Solicitor  General  appearing  for  the
respondent-Central Bureau of Investigation and have
also perused the materials placed on record. 
4) The allegations as against the appellant are with
respect to two aspects.  One is regarding financial
irregularities in the College where the appellant
was the Principal and the other is with regard to
accommodating  undeserving  candidates  through
manipulation of merit scores. 
5) Suffice  it  to  state  that  the  appellant  has
undergone incarceration for more than two years and
we have been informed that only 07 out of 147
witnesses have been examined so far.
6) In such view of the matter, considering the
period of incarceration and also the stage of the
trial, we are inclined to set aside the impugned
order passed by the High Court and allow this
appeal. 
7) Accordingly, the impugned order dated 23.02.2026
passed by the High Court stands set aside, and the
appellant  is  granted  bail  on  such  terms  and
conditions as may be imposed by the concerned Trial
Court.
2

--- Page 416 ---
8) Accordingly, the appeal stands allowed in the
above terms.
9) Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The present petition calls in question the correctness of
the order dated 30-10-2025 in Criminal Misc.Bail Application
No.36210/2025  passed  by  the  High  Court  of  Judicature  at

--- Page 435 ---
2
Allahabad. By the said order, the High Court had enlarged the
respondent no.2-accused on bail in connection with FIR/Case
Crime No.90/2025 registered with Police Station Civil Lines,
District Aligarh, Uttar Pradesh, for the offences punishable
under Sections 2/3 of the Uttar Pradesh Gangsters and Anti-
Social  Activities  (Prevention)  Act,  1986  (for  short,
‘Gangsters Act’)
2. We have heard Mr. Raahul Trivedi, learned counsel for the
petitioner -  defacto complainant, Ms. Ruchira Goel, learned
counsel for the State and Mr. Vivek Singh, learned counsel for
the respondent no.2-accused.
3. Learned counsel for the petitioner - defacto complainant
contends that the High Court has totally overlooked the fact
that there are nine criminal cases which are pending against
the respondent no.2. Learned contends that the State of Uttar
Pradesh in the counter affidavit filed in the matter has set
out the nine criminal cases. However, nothing was brought to
the notice of the High Court. The High Court has recorded that
the AGA could not oppose the prayer for bail and could not
point out any other case against the applicant(re spondent no.2
herein) except the one shown against the Gang-chart.
4. Learned counsel for the State points to paragraph 6 of
the counter affidavit wherein the following criminal history
of the respondent no.2 has been set out:-
S.No. Case Crime No. Sections/Offences
1 306 of 2020 Sections 147, 148, 149 and 302 I.P .C.
2 188 of 2020 Sections 147, 148, 149, 323, 504, 506, 
325 and 307 I.P .C.

--- Page 436 ---
3
3 607 of 2020 Section 2/3 of the U.P .Gangsters and 
Anti-Social Activities (Prevention) Act
4 719 of 2019 Sections 147, 148, 149, 323 and 504 
I.P .C. and Section 3(2)(v) of the 
Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes 
(Prevention of Atrocities) Act
5 13 of 2023 Sections 323, 342, 376, 452, 506 and 34 
I.P .C. and Sections 3/4 of the Protection 
of Children from Sexual Offences Act 
6 442 of 2022 Sections 147, 323 and 506 I.P .C.
7 334 of 2023 Sections 120-B, 307 and 506 I.P .C. and 
Sections 3/25/27 of the Arms Act
8 191 of 2020 Sections 149, 150, 151, 188, 291 and

9 329 of 2024 Sections 191(2), 191(3), 190, 109(1),

of the Arms Act
5. Learned counsel for the respondent no.2-accused, on the
other hand, submits that the impugned order is of 30.10.2025
whereby the respondent no.2 has already been enlarged on bail.
Learned counsel also submits that in all the cases set out in
the chart of counter affidavit, the respondent no.2 is on
bail. Learned counsel submits that respondent no.2 has not
indulged in the criminal act post the grant of bail by the
High Court. Learned counsel further contended that though the
impugned  order  recorded  that  the  counsel  appearing  for
respondent no.2 said that there was no criminal history of the
respondent  no.2,  however,  in  the  bail  application,  the
criminal antecedents were set out.
6. Having considered the submissions of the learned counsel
appearing for the parties, we are of the opinion that the
impugned  order  cannot  be  sustained.  The  impugned  order
deserves to be aside. 

--- Page 437 ---
4
7. The High Court has not been apprised of the criminal
history of the respondent no.2.
8. The High Court has also been misled by the respondent
no.2 during the arguments to the effect that there was no
criminal history for the respondent no.2 except aforesaid Case
Crime No.90/2025.
9. We refrain ourselves to make any further observations
lest it prejudice the case of the respondent no.2. 
10. We are of the opinion that in the above circumstances the
interest of justice requires that the impugned order be set
aside and the matter be remitted to the High Court for fresh
consideration after looking into all the relevant material.
11. Accordingly, the prayer of the petitioner is allowed. We
direct that the impugned order dated 30.10.2025 is set aside
and  the  Criminal  Misc.Bail  Application  No.36210/2025  be
restored to the file of the High Court. 
12. We are conscious that the respondent no.2 has been on
bail since 30.10.2025. However, since the impugned order has
been passed without adverting to any of the criminal history
of the respondent no.2, we direct the respondent no.2 to
surrender to the concerned Police Station/Court on or before
30.10.2026.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION
ARBITRATION PETITION NO. 50 OF 2026
HPCL RAJASTHAN REFINERY 
LIMITED PETITIONER(S)
VERSUS
CHEMIE TECH DMCC RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. This petition under Section 11(6) of the Arbitration and
Conciliation Act, 1996 (Act), seeks the appointment of a sole
arbitrator  to  adjudicate  disputes  arising  from  three  tender
contracts awarded to the Respondent by the Petitioner through
Letters of Acceptance. These tender contracts are namely: (i)
Package 7A dated 06.09.2021; (ii) Package 6A dated 13.11.2021; and
(iii) EPCC-11 dated 13.11.2021 (collectively “Tender Contracts”). 
2. Briefly observed, the Petitioner, HPCL Rajasthan Refinery
Limited, is a public-sector undertaking, which is a joint venture
between Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited and the Government
of Rajasthan. It is engaged in the establishment of an integrated
grassroot refinery-cum-petrochemical complex at Barmer, Rajasthan.
For  the  said  project,  the  Petitioner  floated  three  tender
contracts, namely, Package 7A (double-wall tanks, including dyke
facilities), Package 6A (intermediate and product storage tanks,
tank pads and associated civil works) and EPCC-11 (crude oil
terminal and associated facilities). These were awarded to the
Respondent, Chemie Tech DMCC, a company registered in Dubai, UAE,
1

--- Page 445 ---
which is a subsidiary of Chemie Tech Limited, incorporated in
Jersey, Channel Islands and is engaged in providing engineering,
procurement,  and  construction  (EPC)  solutions  across  various
industries. All the tender contracts are statedly governed by
identical Special Conditions of Contract (SCC). Clause 99.1.2 of
the SCC contains an arbitration clause, which provides for the
resolution of disputes by a Sole Arbitrator, with the seat of
arbitration at New Delhi, India.
3. It appears that a dispute arose when the Respondent allegedly
failed to adhere to various contractual obligations, including,
inter alia, non-furnishing of Contract Performance Bank Guarantees,
and missing project milestones leading to delays and eventual
cessation of work. It is stated that, consequently, the Petitioner
issued Show Cause Notices and thereafter terminated all three
tender contracts vide Termination Notices dated 18.02.2023, which
were disputed by the Respondent. The Petitioner is said to have
awarded replacement contracts for the three projects to other
companies, while raising monetary claims against the Respondent.
4. In these circumstances, the Petitioner sought to initiate
arbitral proceedings under Clause 99.1.2 of the respective SCCs,
prompting it to issue Notice of Arbitration dated 30.01.2026 to the
Respondent. Petitioner suggested the names of three former High
Court  Judges  for  appointment  as  the  Sole  Arbitrator  and  a
consolidated adjudication of the disputes arising under all three
tender  contracts.  However,  the  Respondent,  vide reply  dated
2

--- Page 446 ---
01.03.2026, has declined to consent to the appointment of any of
the suggested persons. It is evident that an attempt of amicable
settlement  between  the  parties  has  also  failed.  Hence,  the
Petitioner has filed the instant Petition under Section 11 of the
Act.
5. We have heard learned counsel for the parties and perused the
material placed on record.
6. Keeping in view the facts and circumstances recorded above and
the relevant provision(s) under the SCCs of the three tender
contracts, we deem it just and proper to allow the instant
Arbitration Petition in the above terms and appoint Justice Indira
Banerjee, former Judge of this Court, as the Sole Arbitrator to
resolve the disputes between the parties arising under the tender
contracts. The seat and venue of arbitration, in accordance with
the arbitration agreement, shall be New Delhi, India. 
7. The  Arbitrator  shall  have  the  liberty  to  fix  her  own
remuneration/fees in consultation with the parties. The fees and

--- Page 450 ---
2
4. Learned Senior counsel appearing for the respondent(s) would

no coercive steps shall be taken against the respondent(s).

Court to expedite the hearing of the matter and make an
endeavour to dispose it of within a period of two months from
the date of receipt of a copy of this order.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL  NO(S).  8217/2011
PONNAMPURATH PADMINI AMMA 
(DEAD THROUGH LRS) & ORS.    APPELLANT(S)
                                VERSUS
KRISHNAN NAIR (DEAD THROUGH LRS) & ORS.            RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. The present appeal has been filed assailing the impugned
judgment dated 23.03.2011, passed by the High Court of
Kerala in RSA No.356/2007(A), wherein, the second appeal
was allowed and matter was remanded back to the Trial
Court for fresh consideration.
2. The respondents-plaintiffs have instituted a suit seeking
partition of the plaint schedule properties and to give
14 out of 16 shares to plaintiff-respondent, together
with mesne profits on the premise that suit properties
are  tharavadu  properties.  The  Trial  Court,  in  O.S.
No.770/1996,  upon hearing the parties, and after going
through the materials available on record, was pleased to
dismiss the suit, inter alia holding that suit properties
are  self-acquired  properties.  On  an  appeal  in  A.S.
No.152/2001, the First Appellate Court has also confirmed
the same. However, in the second appeal, the High Court,

--- Page 460 ---
2
while reversing the findings of the Lower Court, on the
character of the properties, nonetheless was pleased to
remit the matter to the Trial Court to consider the
issues  pertaining  to  adverse  possession,  ouster  and
limitation. Aggrieved by the same, the appellants are
before this Court. 
3. We have heard the learned counsel appearing for the
appellants and the learned counsel appearing for the
respondent Nos.3, 15 and 20. 
4. The contesting respondents, though appeared initially
through a counsel, did not appeared thereafter, despite
the subsequent notice served on them, as earlier learned
counsel relinquished her Vakalatnama. Unfortunately, even
today, there is no representation from the respondents.
On the last occasion also, none was present on behalf of
them. 
5. The appellants are the defendants in the suit O.S.
No.770/1996. The respondent Nos.3, 15 and 20 are the
defendants supporting the case of the appellants.
6. A specific plea has been taken by the appellants as
reflected in the arguments on their behalf, with respect
to the limitation, adverse possession and ouster. 
7. Learned  Senior  Counsel  appearing  for  the  appellants
submit  that  the  finding  of  the  High  Court  on  the
character of the properties has been made by placing
wrong reliance upon the law laid down in ‘ Achuthan Nair

--- Page 461 ---
3
Vs. Chinnamu Amma & Ors.’,  (1966) 1 SCR 454, cannot be
sustained in the eye of law. In any case, the parties
having understood each others case, merely because issues
are not framed, cannot be a ground to remit the matter
back for fresh consideration, especially, when arguments
have been made and specific findings have been rendered,
by taking note of the evidence available on record. 
8. The learned counsel appearing for the respondent Nos.3,
15  and  20  has  also  supported  the  appellants  by
reiterating the aforesaid submissions.
9. Taking note of the submissions made at the Bar, we are
inclined to remit the matter to the High Court for fresh
consideration, as we find that piecemeal approach adopted
by the High Court cannot be sustained in the eye of law. 
10. Law is quite settled on the fact that in the event of
need for further evidence, the same can always be called
for. Furthermore, both the Trial Court and the First
Appellate Court have considered the issue of adverse
possession, ouster and limitation. In fact, this being
the  suit  for  partition,  the  question  of  adverse
possession will not arise, and what we are concerned with
is the ouster. Be that as it may, the High Court ought to
have decided the appeal on merits, in accordance with the
law, after holding the existence of substantial question
of law, which in answer will have the effect of reversing
the judgment and decree of the Trial Court, as confirmed

--- Page 462 ---
4
by the First Appellate Court. 
11. Accordingly, even on the first issue, the High Court is
requested to re-hear the parties, along with the other
issues  pertaining  to  adverse  possession,  ouster  and
limitation. 
12. In such view of the matter, the impugned order stands set
aside, and the matter stands remitted back to the High
Court for fresh consideration. All the issues are left
open. 
13. Needless to state that the High Court, while hearing the
matter, shall not take into consideration any of the
findings  rendered  in  the  impugned  judgment  dated
23.03.2011, which was under challenge in the present
appeal. 
14. The appeal stands disposed of, accordingly.
15. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed
of.

1. We have heard the learned Senior counsel appearing for the
appellant and the learned Senior counsel appearing for the
respondents. 
2. The appellant herein instituted a suit in the year 1988, for
declaration of the right to manage and administer the affairs
of  Sri  Venugopalswamy  Bajanaimadam  and  for  consequential
injunction, which was decreed by the Trial Court vide order
dated 18.09.1995. The High Court, vide order dated 16.12.2009,
in an appeal by the respondents reversed the findings of the
Trial  Court,  by  holding  that  the  suit  itself  was  not
maintainable in the absence of a declaration having been
obtained from the Deputy Commissioner under Section 63(a) of
the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act,

--- Page 465 ---
2
1959 (hereinafter 'the said Act').
3. In the present case, the short issue involved is, as to
whether the judgment and decree of the High Court in holding
that the suit is not maintainable is proper or not. 
4. While concurring with the High Court's conclusion, we are
inclined to hold that there is no need for incidental findings
on facts. In fact the appellant did invoke Section 63(a) of
the said Act, which was dismissed on default. Suffice it is to
state, that in view of the judgment of the High Court, there
is no bar for the appellant to invoke Section 63(a) of the
said Act once again, particularly, by taking note of the fact
that the earlier application was dismissed on default. 
5. In such view of the matter, we are inclined to grant six weeks
time to the appellant from the date of receipt of a copy of
this order to invoke Section 63(a) of the said Act. 
6. Such application being filed before the concerned authority
namely, Joint/Deputy Commissioner, shall be disposed of within
a period of three months thereafter. Till such time, status
quo as of today, shall be maintained by the parties.
7. We make it clear that the competent authority is directed to
decide the application on its own merits and in accordance
with the law, without being influenced by any of the findings
on merit rendered by the High Court in the impugned judgment. 
8. The appeal stands disposed of, in the aforesaid terms and with
aforementioned directions.

father  of  the  deceased  alleging  telephonic  information
regarding death of his daughter by hanging was received.
1

--- Page 475 ---
On the same day, appellant came to be arrested and has
remained  in  custody  till  date.  After  completion  of  the
investigation, chargesheet has been filed against parents
of  the  appellant  and  the  appellant  (husband)  herein.
Undisputedly,  the  parents  of  the  appellant  have  been
granted bail.
5. Having heard the learned counsels appearing for the
parties and on perusal of the records, we notice that the
father of the deceased – complainant has turned hostile
during trial or in other words, he has not supported the
prosecution’s case. It is at this juncture, the mother of the
deceased is said to have filed an application to get herself
examined and said application is said to be pending before
trial court. It is for the trial court to take a call on the said
application. Be that as it may, we have not expressed any
opinion in that regard.
6. Having  regard  to  the  fact  that  parents  of  the
appellant have been enlarged on bail and the likelihood of
trial being concluded in the near future being bleak and out
of  thirty-five  witnesses,  only  four  witnesses  have  been
2

--- Page 476 ---
examined, we are of the considered view that appellant
would  be  entitled  for  being  released  on  bail  as  his

make it clear that in the event of any adjournment being
sought for by the appellant without any justifiable cause to
the satisfaction of the trial court, the prosecution would be
at liberty to move the trial court for cancellation of the bail.
Wit this observation, the appeal stands allowed.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL  NO. 112 OF 2017
BALARAM DANDAPAT                                            APPELLANT
VERSUS
THE STATE OF ODISHA & ORS.                             RESPONDENTS
O R D E R
1. Appellant’s  original  application 1 before  the  Orissa
Administrative  Tribunal  succeeded.  The  order  dated
16.03.2012 inter alia recorded as follows:
“It  is  also  admitted  that  respondent  No.4,  Rama
Chandra Sahoo, has resorted to fraud by posing as a SC
candidate  though  he  is  not  a  SC  candidate  and  his
Schedule  Caste  certificate  has  not  been  issued  by  the
authority competent to issue such certificate. Hence, said
Rama Chandra Sahoo be reverted from the promotional
post of the District Fisheries Officer of the SC category
after resorting to due procedure as prescribed in the case
of  Kumari  Madhuri  Patil  v/s  Addl.  Commissioner  Tribal
Development,  AIR  1995  SC  94,  and  promotion  of  the
applicant as per merit-cum-suitability with due regard to
seniority be considered in a properly reconvened as per
Rule-8(1) of the Orissa Fisheries Service (Recruitment and
Conditions  of  Service)  Rules,  1977  and  in  the  case
applicant  is  deemed  suitable,  the  applicant  should  be
allowed  notional  promotion  from  the  date  of  Sri  Rama
Chandra Sahoo, Respondent No.4, was promoted. Actual
financial benefits shall, however, accrue to him only on his
1 O.A.No.1726 of 2008
1

--- Page 509 ---
assuming  superior  charge.  This  order  be  implemented
within a period of three months from the date of receipt.”
2. The said order of the Tribunal was reversed by the
High  Court  by  its  order  dated  05.07.2016,  which  is  the
subject matter of challenge in this appeal by special leave
granted on 03.01.2017.
3. We have heard Mr. Manish Singhvi, learned senior
counsel appearing for the appellant and have perused the
orders passed by the Tribunal as well as the High Court.
4. There  is  nothing  on  record  to  indicate,  much  less
admission  of  any  party,  that  the  respondent  no.4 2 had
obtained a scheduled caste certificate by resorting to fraud.
On the contrary, there is material on record to suggest that
no proceeding was initiated for the purpose of examining
the validity of the scheduled caste certificate of the said
respondent in terms of the decision of this Court in Kumari
Madhuri  Patil  v.  Addl.  Commissioner  Tribal
Development3. 
5. Thus, the main plank resting on which the Tribunal
had  allowed  the  application  of  the  appellant,  i.e.,  an
erroneous assumption that the respondent no.4 resorted to
fraud, has no foundation in law or on record. The High Court
2 Rama Chandra Sahoo
3 AIR 1995 SC 94
2

--- Page 510 ---
did not commit any error in allowing the writ petition of
respondent no.4.
6. There  is  absolutely  no  merit  in  this  appeal  which
stands dismissed. 
.................................…J.
(DIPANKAR DATTA)
................................…J.
       (SHEEL NAGU)

OCTOBER 15, 2026.

application  by  the  High  Court  of  Gujarat  at

appellant is before us.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.       OF 2026
(ARISING OUT OF S.L.P. (CRL.) NO.16803 OF 2026)
TRIVENDRA       ...Appellant
VERSUS
STATE OF U.P.  ...Respondent
O R D E R
1) Leave granted.
2) The appellant has been implicated as an accused
in connection with F.I.R. No.05 of 2021 registered
at P.S.-Syana, District-Bulandshahr, Uttar Pradesh
and  has  been  chargesheeted  for  the  offences
punishable under Sections 304B, 498A, 323, 504 and
506 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short, ‘the
IPC’) and Sections 3 and 4 of the Dowry Prohibition
Act, 1961.  Aggrieved by the rejection of the bail
application by the High Court of Judicature at
Allahabad, Uttar Pradesh vide impugned order dated
29.04.2026  passed  in  Criminal  Misc.  Bail
Application No.14310 of 2026, the appellant is
before us. 
3) We have heard the learned counsel appearing for
the parties and have also perused the material
placed on record. 
1

--- Page 529 ---
4) The appellant is the husband of the deceased-
victim.  The case of the prosecution is that the
appellant lit the fire leading to death of the
deceased-victim due to burn injuries. 
5) The learned counsel appearing for the respondent-
State would submit that the dying declaration of
the deceased-victim implicates the appellant and,
in fact, the appellant has absconded earlier.  
6) Suffice it to state that the appellant has been
under incarceration for more than two and a half
years, and the trial is still going on wherein,
only few material witnesses have been examined. 
7) In such view of the matter, we are inclined to
set aside the impugned order passed by the High
Court on the premise that the appellant has been
under incarceration for a period of more than two
and  a  half  years,  and  also  that  continued
incarceration of the appellant is not required.   
8) Hence, the impugned order dated 29.04.2026 passed
by  the  High  Court  in  Criminal  Misc.  Bail
Application No.14310 of 2026 stands set aside and
the appellant is granted bail on such terms and
conditions as may be imposed by the concerned Trial
Court.
2

--- Page 530 ---
9) Accordingly, the appeal stands allowed in the
above terms.
10) Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL  NO.       OF 2026
(@ SLP(CRL.) No.15782/2026)
MAHENDRA SINGH KORI & ORS.                         APPELLANT(S)
                                VERSUS
STATE OF UTTAR PRADESH & ORS.                      RESPONDENT(S)
 
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard the learned Senior counsel appearing for the
parties. 
3. In the present appeal, the proceedings arise out of the FIR
bearing Case Crime No.280 of 2022 for the offences punishable
under Sections 420, 467, 468, 471, 384 and 120B of the Indian
Penal Code, 1860 and Section 3(1)(f) of the Scheduled Castes
and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989
(hereinafter referred to as 'the SC/ST Act').
4. It is pertinent to note that Section 15A of the SC/ST Act
provides the rights of victims and witnesses. Section 15A(5)
particularly, entitles the victim or his dependent(s) to be
heard  in  respect  of  proceedings  against  the  accused.
Admittedly, in the present case, the statutory mandate of

--- Page 545 ---
2
Section 15A has not been complied with, as the High Court
proceeded to quash the criminal proceedings without affording
an opportunity for the victim to be heard. 
5. Though,  the  learned  Senior  counsel  appearing  for  the
respondent(s) submitted that the entire complaint is vexatious
and is an abuse of the process, we are not inclined to go into
the merits of the case in view of the non-compliance of the
statutory mandate under Section 15A of the SC/ST Act. 
6. We are also conscious of the earlier order passed by us. 
7. In such view of the matter, the impugned order stands set
aside, only on the ground of non-compliance of the statutory
mandate under Section 15A of the SC/ST Act.
8. We are inclined to remand back the matter to the High Court,
for fresh reconsideration, after affording an opportunity for
hearing the victim
9. We make it clear that all other issues are left open to be
decided in the appropriate proceedings, in accordance with
law. 
10. Taking note of the aforesaid circumstances, we request the
High Court to make an endeavour to decide the matter, within a
period of three months from the date of receipt of a copy of
this order.  
11. The  appeal  stands  disposed  of,  with  the  aforesaid
observations.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.                     OF 2026
(@SLP(CRL.) NO.13280 OF 2026)
MOHAMMAD AARIF ABDUL RAZAK SAMOL  ..... APPELLANT(S)
              VERSUS
STATE OF GUJARAT ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. Appellant has been arraigned as an accused for the offences punishable
under  Sections  5(1),  6(b),  8(2),  8(4)  and  10  of  the  Gujarat  Animal
Preservation Act, 2011, under Section 325 of the BNS and Section 119 of
the Gujarat Police Act.
4. The sum and substance of the prosecution case is that appellant illegally
procured 23 kgs of cow meat transported in a swift car and stored it in an
open plot near his house for retail sale and after police conducted a raid,
appellant is said to have fled from the scene. Hence, he has been arrested
on 03.01.2026 and is in custody till date.
5. Learned  counsel  appearing  for  the  respondent-State  vehemently
opposed the grant of bail and contended that trial is at the fag end and
would be concluded expeditiously namely within a period of two months
from today. She would also submit that appellant is having five antecedents
1                                                                                          SLP(CRL.) NO.13280 OF 2026

--- Page 549 ---
of similar nature and, if enlarged on bail, he is likely to indulge in similar
acts. As such, she prays for dismissal of the appeal.
6. Learned  counsel appearing for  the  appellant would submit that the
prosecution  case  is  based  entirely  on  circumstantial  evidence  and
presumptions. He would submit that appellant is not arrested at the spot
and the meat was recovered from an open space which was accessible by
one and all and the said plot was not owned by appellant. Even the swift
car which is alleged to have been used for transportation, does not belong
to him.
7. Having  heard  the  learned  counsels  appearing  for  the  parties  and
noticing that appellant has been in custody for more than eight months, as
also the fact that alleged meat was recovered from an open plot, of course
near the house of the appellant, and charge-sheet having been filed and
trial has already commenced, his continued incarceration would not be
warranted. As to the complicity of appellant in the alleged procurement
and storage of meat, requires to be established by the prosecution by
examining their witnesses. Merely because the appellant’s antecedents are
there, would not be definitive proof of guilt in the present case. Hence,
without expressing any opinion on merits we are of the considered view
that appellant is entitled for being released on regular bail.
8. Hence, we allow the appeal and set aside the impugned order. Appellant
is ordered to be released on regular bail on such terms and conditions as
the jurisdictional Court may deem fit to impose.
2                                                                                          SLP(CRL.) NO.13280 OF 2026

--- Page 550 ---
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.            OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO.15904/2026)
SATISH KUMAR @ BICHHU      APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
STATE OF HIMACHAL PRADESH         RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant and
learned  counsel  for  the  respondent-State  of  Himachal
Pradesh.
3. Appellant is aggrieved by order dated 23.07.2026
passed by the High Court of Himachal Pradesh at Shimla
(briefly the ‘High Court’ hereinafter), rejecting the
application filed by the appellant for suspension of
sentence and grant of bail during pendency of the appeal
before the High Court.
4. Appellant was convicted by the Special Judge, Mandi
in NDPS Case No.55 of 2023 under Section 29 read with
Section  20(b)(ii)(C)  of  the  Narcotics  Drugs  and
Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 (for short, ‘NDPS Act’)
1

--- Page 569 ---
vide the judgment and order dated 11.11.2024. Consequently
by order dated 03.12.2024, appellant was sentenced to
undergo Rigorous Imprisonment (for short, ‘RI’) for a
period of 12 years and to pay fine of Rs.1,20,000/- with a
default stipulation.
5. Aggrieved by the aforesaid conviction and sentence,
appellant has preferred an appeal before the High Court,
being Criminal Appeal No.172 of 2025. Appellant also filed
an application under Section 430 of the Bharatiya Nagarik
Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (for short, ‘BNSS’), being Cr. MP
No.1397 of 2026, for suspension of sentence and grant of
bail.
6. By the impugned order dated 23.07.2026, the High
Court has rejected the aforesaid application, by a very
long order running into 58 pages.
7. We feel that by such a long order, the appeal itself
could have been disposed of.
8. Be  that as  it may,  we find  that as  of today,
appellant has undergone almost 5 and a half years of
incarceration out of the total sentence of 12 years. The
pending appeal pending before the High Court is of the
year 2025 and is not likely to be heard in the immediate
future.
9. That being the position, we suspend the sentence
imposed on the appellant and direct that he shall be
released on bail on usual terms and conditions. However,
the appellant shall co-operate with the hearing of the
2

--- Page 570 ---
appeal.
10. Accordingly, the Criminal Appeal is allowed.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand
disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.              OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO. 14695/2026)
ANIMESH KUMAR      APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
THE STATE OF BIHAR       RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant and
learned counsel for the respondent-State of Bihar.
3. This  appeal  takes  exception  to  the  order  dated
02.07.2026 passed by the High Court of Judicature at Patna
(briefly the ‘High Court’ hereinafter), rejecting the
prayer for anticipatory bail of the appellant.
4. Appellant has been arrayed as an accused in FIR
No.163/2026  registered  at  Police  Station-  Ramkrishna
Nagar, District- Patna, Bihar under Sections 21, 22(b) and
22(c) of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances
Act, 1985 (for short, ‘NDPS Act’).
5. Allegation  against  the  appellant  is  that  police
raided the house of the appellant. At that time, one Rohit
Kumar was loading the contraband onto a vehicle. The
1

--- Page 573 ---
contraband  included  10,500  ampoules  of  Buprenorphine
injections, total 6.3 grams, and 7,750 bottles of codeine
based cough syrup, weighing 1550 grams. It is from the
vehicle that the contraband was recovered and seized.
6. This  Court,  in  paragraph  4  of  the  order  dated
14.08.2026,  had  granted  interim  protection  to  the
appellant subject to the appellant co-operating with the
investigation, whereafter notice was issued on 03.09.2026,
pursuant to which respondent-State of Bihar has filed
counter affidavit.
7. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that the
house from where Rohit Kumar was apprehended pertains to
his mother. Appellant is a teacher and resides in a
different locality. He has no connection at all with the
recovery and seizure of the contraband, not to speak of
any recovery made from his possession. He further submits
that pursuant to the interim protection granted by this
Court, he has co-operated with the investigation.
8. Learned counsel for the respondent-State of Bihar,
very  fairly,  submits  that  appellant  has  joined
investigation.
9. Considering the above, we are of the view that the
interim protection granted by this Court vide the order
dated 14.08.2026 should be made absolute.
10. That being the position, we set aside the impugned
order dated 02.07.2026 passed by the High Court and make
paragraph  4  of  the  order  dated  14.08.2026  absolute.
2

--- Page 574 ---
However, the appellant shall continue to co-operate with
the investigation of the case.
11. Consequently, the Criminal Appeal is allowed.
12. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL  NO.         OF 2026
(@ SLP(C) No.33597/2026)
THE STATE OF MAHARASHTRA & ORS.                 APPELLANT(S)
                                VERSUS
M/S GURUNANK DIARY AND SWEETS 
A PROPRIETARY CONCERN, & ORS.    RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The present appeal has been filed assailing the judgment dated
17.08.2026 passed by the Division Bench of High Court of
Bombay in Writ Petition No. 9905/2026, whereby, the suspension
of respondent No.1 – Dairy's license for food was set aside.
Vide the impugned order, respondent No.1 was further permitted
to resume its business, and the petitioners were directed to
compensate a sum of Rs.5,00,000/- to the respondent No.1 for
loss of revenue, due to the suspension of its food license.
3. We are inclined to consider the issue with respect to the
imposition of costs of Rs. 5,00,000/- alone. 
4. In our considered view, the High Court has erred in directing
the payment of compensation, especially, when the Food Safety

--- Page 601 ---
2
and Standards Act, 2006 involves a bonafide action. The High
Court has mis-construed the facts. In our considered view, the
order of suspension was passed in the official capacity. We
also find that the direction for payment of costs cannot be
sustained in the teeth of Regulation 2.1.8(5) of the Food
Safety  and  Standards  (Licensing  and  Registration  of  Food
Businesses) Regulations, 2011. 
5. Taking note of the aforesaid, the impugned order stands aside
only with respect to the imposition of costs in the nature of
compensation. 
6. The appeal stands disposed of, in the aforesaid terms.
7. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.1172/2012
CHIEF GENERAL MANAGER, BSNL  APPELLANT
                                VERSUS
COLLECTOR OF CENTRAL EXCISE, BHOPAL RESPONDENTS
O R D E R
1. The issues involved in this appeal relates to classification
of the product steel tubular transmission poles (Hamilton poles or
tubes) manufactured by Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited (for short
“BSNL”) for the purpose of levy of Central Excise Duty, namely,
whether  the  goods  are  classifiable  under  heading  7308.90
(structures / parts of structures, eligible for exemption) or
under heading 7306.90 (tubes and pipes). Same is no more  res
integra in view of the law laid down by this Court in the matter
of India Metals and Ferro Alloys Ltd., Cuttack Vs. Collector of
Central Excise, Bhubaneswar, 1991 Supp (1) SCC 125.
2. However, the learned counsel appearing for the appellant, by
drawing our attention to the circular No.A-28/1990 dated 27.09.1990
at Annexure-A1 would contend that the goods in question was
classified under sub-heading 7308.90, which was later changed by
circular  dated  06.09.2000  vide  Circular  No.545/41/2000-CX  at
Annexure-A5. As such, the levy for the month of July and August,
2000  would  amount  to  retrospective  application,  which  is
impermissible, and this fact has not been considered by the
1

--- Page 605 ---
authorities as well as by the Appellate Tribunal, namely, CESTAT.
Hence, the learned counsel appearing for the appellant has prayed
for same being set aside and levy being quashed, at least for the
months of July and August, 2000.
3. Per contra , Mr.  Raghavendra P Shankar , learned Additional
Solicitor General of India appearing for the respondent, would
support the impugned order and contends that the show cause notice
itself is of the year 2001, and by circular dated 06.09.2000, the
department has only reiterated the law laid down by this Court in
India Metals and Ferro Alloys Ltd., Cuttack  referred to supra.
Hence, the question of retrospectivity would not arise.
4. Having heard the learned advocates appearing for the parties,
and on perusal of the records, we are of the considered view that
the contention raised by the learned counsel appearing for the
appellant does not hold water.
5. A perusal of the show cause notice dated 25.07.2001 would
clearly indicate that it is issued subsequent to the circular dated
06.09.2000, and even in the said circular, what has been stated is
reiteration of the law laid down by this Court, namely, the goods
in question is classifiable under the sub-heading 7306.90 and not
under  7308.90.  As  such,  the  question  of  the  levy  being
retrospectively being applied does not arise.
6. Even otherwise also, it can be noticed that this Court in the
above-referred judgment has clearly held that the goods in question
is classifiable under the sub-heading 7306.90, which judgment came
to be rendered on 22.11.1990 and as such, the show cause notice
issued on 25.07.2001 relating to levy for the period of July and
2

--- Page 606 ---
August, 2000 cannot be construed or held as being retrospectively.
In that view of the matter also, we are of the considered view that
there is no merit in this appeal. Accordingly, it stands dismissed.
7. Pending applications, if any, stands disposed of. Costs made
easy.
.................J.
  (ARAVIND KUMAR)
.................J.
(VIPUL M. PANCHOLI)
NEW DELHI;
JULY 16, 2026.

regular bail application by the High Court of

is before us.

offence  was  committed  way  back  in  the  year

2015 i.e., more than a decade ago.

granted bail on such terms and conditions as may be

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO(S).        OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CIVIL) NO(S). 5534/2025)
SWETHA TN AND ANOTHER                                APPELLANT(S)
                                VERSUS
UNITED INDIA INSURANCE COMPANY LTD. AND ORS.        RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
Leave granted.
2. Heard learned counsel appearing for the parties.
3. The present appeal arises out of the judgment and order dated
12.03.2024 passed by the High Court of Karnataka at Bengaluru in
Miscellaneous First Appeal No. 1325 of 2020 (MV-D), whereby the
compensation awarded to the appellants/claimants by the Motor
Accident  Claims  Tribunal  was  enhanced  by  an  amount  of
Rs.1,22,36,044/-,  taking  the  total  compensation  to
Rs.1,37,24,044/-, with interest at the rate of 6% per annum from
the date of filing of the claim petition till realization.
4.  Upon  perusing  the  impugned  judgment  and  considering  the
submissions made on behalf of the parties, we find that the
compensation  has  been  correctly  assessed  by  the  High  Court.
However, we find no justification for reducing the rate of interest
from 9% to 6% per annum. The rate of interest ordinarily awarded by
this Court in such matters is 7.5% per annum.

--- Page 722 ---
2
5. Having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case, we
consider it appropriate to award interest at the rate of 7.5% per
annum.
6. Accordingly, the impugned judgment is modified to the extent
that the rate of interest on the compensation awarded by the High
Court shall stand enhanced from 6% to 7.5% per annum, from the date
of filing of the claim petition till realization.
7. The appeal stands allowed to the extent indicated above.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
Heard learned counsel for the petitioner and learned
counsel for the respondent-State and perused the material
available on record.
1

--- Page 800 ---
This special leave petition is directed against the
judgment dated 17 th September, 2024, passed by the High
Court of Jharkhand at Ranchi in Criminal Appeal (DB) No.
999 of 2018.  
The petitioner was tried by the learned District &
Additional Sessions Judge-II, Giridih, in Sessions Trial
No. 63 of 2012 and was convicted for the offence punishable
under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal
Code, 1860. He was sentenced to undergo imprisonment for
life and to pay a fine of Rs. 30,000/-.  The charge against
the  petitioner  was  that  he  had  set  his  own  wife,
Smt. Sushma Devi, on fire, resulting in her death.
The prosecution case was primarily based on the
depositions of the two minor children of the petitioner and
the deceased Sushma Devi, namely, Master R (PW-1) and
Master A (PW-2).  Both the witnesses categorically deposed
that their father, i.e., the petitioner herein and the
other family members, started beating their mother.  The
petitioner  exhorted  that  he  would  kill  Sushma  Devi.
Kerosene oil was brought and sprinkled over the body of the
victim,  and  the  petitioner  set  her  on  fire  with  a
matchstick.  
On going through the evidence of both child witnesses
(supra), we do not find anything which can persuade us that
the witnesses were, in any manner, tutored or that their
testimony  suffered  from  any  infirmity,  discrepancy  or
material contradiction.  The trial Court as well as the
2

--- Page 801 ---
High  Court  have  assigned  cogent  reasons,  after  due
appreciation  of  the  evidence  available  on  record  in
convicting the petitioner and affirming his conviction.
We  find  no  merit  in  the  instant  special  leave
petition, which is dismissed as such.
Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.
(KRITIKA TIWARI)                              (AKSHAY KUMAR BHORIA)

The petitioner herein was tried and convicted for
the offences punishable under Section 302 of the Indian
Penal Code, 1860, Sections 27 and 30 of the Arms Act,
1959, and was sentenced to imprisonment for life and fine
1

--- Page 824 ---
Diary No.38908/2025
of  Rs.  20,000/-  with  default  stipulation.  The  appeal
preferred by the petitioner herein stands dismissed by the
Division  Bench  of  the  High  Court  of  Uttarakhand  at
Nainital vide judgment dated 23rd February, 2021.
We  have  heard  and  considered  the  submissions
advanced by learned counsel for the petitioner and have
gone  through  the  impugned  judgments  and  the  material
available on record.
Allegation against the petitioner is of shooting his
own wife Smt. Hema Mehta, and thereby, killing her. The
prosecution case is primarily based on the testimony of
two sons of the petitioner and the deceased, namely,
Master U and Master M.
We have been taken through the statements of these
two witnesses by learned counsel for the petitioner and
find that both the child witnesses, stood firm on the
version that they saw their father, the petitioner herein,
shooting their mother dead. The witnesses were cross-
examined at length but could not be shaken. 
We are, therefore, of the opinion that the trial
Court committed no error whatsoever in placing reliance on
the testimony of the two eye-witnesses which stands fully
corroborated by the evidence of Dr. D.S. Dharmashaktu, the
Medical Officer who conducted the postmortem and opined
that the cause of death was gunshot injury on the head of
the deceased.
2

--- Page 825 ---
Diary No.38908/2025
The  impugned  judgment  does  not  suffer  from  any
infirmity  warranting  interference.  Hence,  the  Special

disposed of.

1. The submission on behalf of the petitioner is that the

for the simple reason that a different version of the question
was promptly reported and the impugned First Information Report
was grossly delayed.
1

--- Page 856 ---
2. It prima facie appears that the First Information Report
of which quashing was sought is a cross version of the
incident. Besides,  the  High  Court  has  noticed  that  the
petitioner before the High Court had criminal history of 28
cases and delay was sought to be explained by stating that out
of fear the other side could not promptly register the report
despite effort.
3. Having regard to the above, we decline to interfere with
the impugned order. However, we leave it open to the petitioner
to take recourse to appropriate remedy for clubbing of the two
proceedings in case they are cross versions of each other.
4. Subject to above, the petition is dismissed.

O R D E R
1. Delay condoned.
2. It  is  the  contention  of  learned  counsel  for  the
petitioners that on an application moved under Section 489
of  the  Bharatiya  Nagarik  Suraksha  Sanhita,  2023
(hereinafter referred to as "the BNSS, 2023") for discharge
of sureties given by the petitioners, the Court insisted
upon the personal appearance of the accused person for whom
the surety was given. Learned counsel submits that the
inability to produce the accused was explicitly expressed
1

--- Page 1012 ---
in the application along with the reasons therefor.
3. It is further submitted that under Section 489(2) of
the BNSS, 2023, once an application for discharge of surety
is filed, it is the duty of the Magistrate/Court to issue a
warrant of arrest directing that the accused person be
brought before the Court, which the Court below failed to
resort to.
4. Learned counsel submits that the petitioners would move
an appropriate application in this regard before the Trial
Court, and prays that the Trial Court may be directed to
decide the same in accordance with law.
5. The contentions raised by learned counsel for the
petitioners  are  accepted.  Liberty  is  granted  to  the
petitioners to move an appropriate application before the
Trial Court/Magistrate under Section 489(2) of the BNSS,
2023.  Upon  such  application  being  filed,  the  learned
Magistrate shall forthwith proceed to issue warrants and
take  further  steps  in  accordance  with  the  statutory
provisions and law.
6. Accordingly, the Special Leave Petition stands disposed
of.
7. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The present petition arises out of the impugned judgment and
order dated 07.09.2026 passed by the High Court of Delhi in Bail
Application  No.  283/2025  (along  with  Bail  Application  No.

--- Page 1158 ---
2
293/2025), whereby the High Court affirmed the order of the learned
ASJ-06,  Patiala  House  Courts,  New  Delhi,  and  dismissed  the
petitioner's application seeking anticipatory bail. 
2. The petitioner faces an apprehension of arrest in connection
with FIR No. 237/2024 registered on 22.10.2024 at Police Station
Vasant Kunj North, South West Delhi, for offences punishable under
Sections 420, 468, 471 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860.
3. Learned counsel appearing on behalf of the petitioner submits
that the entire transaction arises out of a commercial/business
relationship between long-standing acquaintances and neighbours. 
4. Learned Counsel for the Respondent-State vehemently opposes
the grant of pre-arrest bail.
5. Having heard learned counsel for the parties and having
perused the material on record, without expressing any opinion on
the merits of the case, we are of the view that the petitioner has
made out a case for the grant of anticipatory bail.
6. Accordingly, it is ordered that in the event of the arrest of
the petitioner (Pankaj Sharma) in connection with FIR No. 237/2024,
P.S. Vasant Kunj North, South West Delhi, he shall be released on
anticipatory bail subject to the conditions the I.O. may deem fit
to impose, on condition also of continued cooperation in the
investigation.
7. Once the petitioner is released on bail by the I.O., on
directions  issued  by  the  I.O.  or  summons  issued  by  the
jurisdictional  court,  the  petitioner  shall  appear  before  the
jurisdictional  court  and  furnish  bail  bonds  and  ensure  due
appearance in the trial. 
8. With the aforesaid, the Special Leave Petition is disposed of.
9. Pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.
 (VISHAL ANAND)                                   (POOJA SHARMA)
DEPUTY REGISTRAR                                 COURT MASTER (NSH)

    Mr. Pashupati Nath Rajdan, AOR
    
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. On perusal of the material available in the Special
Leave Petition paper book, it appears that respondent Nos.2
and 3 were granted temporary bail by the High Court for 21
days vide its order dated 23.01.2026 and since thereafter,
the  temporary  bail  has  been  extended  at  least  on  11
1

--- Page 1166 ---
occasions.
2. The above temporary bail was granted to respondent
Nos.2 and 3 on the ground that their father, Surendra Kumar
Sharma, aged about 89 years, is suffering from some ailment
as mentioned in the order dated 23.01.2026.
3. Mr.  Mrigendra  Singh ,  learned  Senior  Advocate,
submits  that  the  health  condition  of  the  father  of
respondent Nos.2 and 3 is now satisfactory and therefore,
continuation of temporary bail is not at all needed.
4. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case,
instead of keeping the Special Leave Petition  pending, we
dispose of the same by directing that the High Court shall
consider and decide the prayer of respondent Nos.2 and 3 for
continuing the temporary bail within a period of one month
from today.
5. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

This special leave petition was filed assailing the order
passed by the High Court rejecting the appeal filed by the
petitioner-Corporation under Section 37 of the Arbitration and
Conciliation Act, 19961, on the ground of the delay of 59 days in
the filing of the said appeal. However, it is now stated by the
1  For short ‘1996 Act’

--- Page 1354 ---
learned counsel for the petitioner-corporation that, in terms of
the Notification in S.O. No. 351 dated 02.08.2019 issued by the
Government of Bihar, the appeal under Section 37 of the 1996 Act
did not lie before the High Court and the proper forum was the
concerned District Judge’s Court. 
Learned  counsel  appearing  for  the  petitioner-corporation,
therefore, seeks permission to withdraw this special leave petition
reserving liberty to the petitioner to file an appeal before the
appropriate forum in accordance with law. 
Permission granted.

aforestated liberty. However, we may also clarify that we make no
comment in that regard.

1

--- Page 1442 ---

Court.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
We are not inclined to interfere on the legal  issue
qua the interpretation of Sections 5 and 29(2) of the
Limitation Act, 1963.  However, we specifically take
note of the concern expressed by the learned A.S.G that
the delay is being mechanically condoned for a project
which concluded eight years back without even going into
the issue of the extent of delay.
Contd..

--- Page 1480 ---
- 2 - 
Taking note of the said submission, we direct the
concerned Court that,  while considering application for
condonation of delay, the concerned Court should satisfy
itself on the  sufficiency of the reasons assigned, by
way  of  a  reasoned  order,  instead  of  mechanically
condoning the delay by a one line order.
Accordingly,  the  Special  Leave  Petitions  are
disposed of, in the aforesaid terms.
Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand
disposed of. 
(NEETU SACHDEVA)                                (POONAM VAID)
DEPUTY REGISTRAR                              ASSISTANT  REGISTRAR
